articles.title: Pixel 11 Pro : la fonction Pixel Glow pourrait finalement changer de nom
articles.text:
D’abord repérée dans une version bêta d’Android 17, la fonction lumineuse imaginée par Google pourrait ne pas conserver le nom « Pixel Glow » au moment de son lancement. Le constructeur aurait finalement opté pour une appellation plus courte, qui joue directement sur le fonctionnement de cette nouveauté.
Le géant de Mountain View pourrait revoir le nom de l’une des fonctions matérielles les plus attendues sur ses prochains smartphones haut de gamme. Apparue pour la première fois dans la bêta d’Android 17 sous l’appellation « Pixel Glow », cette fonctionnalité lumineuse serait désormais désignée sous le nom de « HiLight », selon Dylan Roussel.
« HiLight », un nom qui joue sur les mots
Le changement de nom ne serait évidemment pas anodin. « HiLight » est construit à partir de « Hi », qui signifie « salut » ou « bonjour » en anglais, et de « Light », qui désigne la lumière. Le terme peut donc se comprendre littéralement comme « Hi Light », soit une manière de dire « Salut, lumière ». L’écriture particulière du nom, avec un « H » et un « L » en majuscules, renforcerait justement l'idée derrière ce jeu de mots.
Cette appellation ferait également référence au rôle de la fonction. La lumière doit notamment permettre de mettre en avant les appels de contacts favoris et les interactions avec Gemini. Le nom fait simplement écho à la lumière physique et à sa manière d’attirer l’attention de l’utilisateur.
Une lumière intégrée à la Camera Bar du Pixel 11 Pro
Les premières traces de Pixel Glow avaient été découvertes en avril dernier, avec la publication d'Android 17 Beta 4. Les paramètres préliminaires de la fonction décrivaient un dispositif capable d’utiliser « une lumière et des couleurs discrètes à l’arrière de l’appareil pour vous informer d’une activité importante lorsque celui-ci est posé face contre table ».
Deux types d'utilisation étaient alors mentionnés dans les réglages. Le premier concerne les appels entrants provenant de contacts ajoutés aux favoris, signalés par des effets lumineux discrets. Le second est, quant à lui, lié aux échanges avec Gemini en mode mains libres, avec un retour visuel destiné à accompagner ces interactions.
Les deux teasers publiés par Google ont par ailleurs montré le fonctionnement de cette lumière sur le Pixel 11 Pro. Celle-ci apparaît aux côtés du flash, directement intégrée à la Camera Bar. Elle pourrait afficher l’ensemble du spectre des couleurs et proposer un effet rotatif qui rappelle visuellement la roue multicolore du Mac lors de certaines opérations.
Il est néanmoins important de rappeler qu'à l'heure actuelle le nom « HiLight » n’a pas encore été officiellement confirmé par Google. Une autre question reste également en suspens : les applications tierces pourront-elles exploiter cette lumière, ou son utilisation sera-t-elle réservée aux fonctionnalités et services de Google ?

articles.title: Vous pouvez désormais louer les vélos électriques Gaya : prix, assurance et prise en charge, ce qu'il faut savoir
articles.text:
Le vélo cargo électrique reste un achat qui se réfléchit au vu des prix d’appel qui oscillent généralement entre 2 500 et 3 000 euros : chez Gaya, il faut compter au minimum 2 300 euros pour un modèle neuf, mais la note grimpe mécaniquement dès qu’on ajoute des accessoires.
À partir de 89 euros par mois
Fondée en 2021 par Amélie Guicheney et Jacques Bonneville, la marque parisienne mise donc sur la location longue durée pour élargir sa clientèle, avec une formule proposée en boutique comme sur son site, apprend-on dans un communiqué de presse envoyé à la rédaction.
Après l’euphorie post-Covid, le marché du vélo électrique a tourné au ralenti partout dans le monde et particulièrement en Europe. Dans ce contexte, proposer la location longue durée plutôt que le seul achat comptant permet d’abaisser le ticket d’entrée et de viser ceux qui hésitent encore à dépenser plusieurs milliers d’euros d’un coup.
Dans le détail, la mensualité de 89 euros – celle sur laquelle Gaya communique – correspond au modèle L’Original Le Court, financé sur 36 mois avec un apport de départ équivalent à deux mensualités. L’assurance casse et vol est comprise, ce que Gaya présente comme l’équivalent du coût d’un abonnement de transport mensuel.
Les accessoires font monter les prix
À noter que les 89 euros correspondent au prix d’appel, sans le moindre accessoire. Dès lors que l’on ajoute une option payante, la mensualité monte : sur l’Original Le Court, un kit Junior facturé 240 euros à l’achat fait passer la note à 98 euros par mois. Les autres modèles suivent la même logique, avec des tarifs à partir de 108 euros pour l’Original Le Long, 112 euros pour l’Incroyable Le Court et 141 euros pour l’Incroyable Le Long. La durée d’engagement, elle, se choisit entre 12, 18, 24, 30 ou 36 mois.
Côté assurance, la garantie couvre jusqu’à deux casses et un vol par an, batterie comprise, avec une franchise de 10 % en cas de sinistre. L’offre est ouverte aux particuliers majeurs et aux professionnels installés dans l’Union européenne, sur présentation de quelques justificatifs (identité, domicile, RIB). Les salariés dont l’entreprise a mis en place le Forfait Mobilités Durables peuvent, eux, affecter ce dispositif employeur au financement d’une partie de l’abonnement.

articles.title: Errant SpaceX rocket stage set to smash into the moon at 5,400 mph, seven times the speed of sound — NASA and South Korean orbiters prepare to track 3-ton TNT impact
articles.text:
Errant SpaceX rocket stage set to smash into the moon at 5,400 mph, seven times the speed of sound — NASA and South Korean orbiters prepare to track 3-ton TNT impact
You really shouldn't leave your trash orbiting in space.
The upper stage of a SpaceX rocket that delivered two lunar landers in early 2025 is set to come crashing down on the lunar surface several months after it ended its mission. According to Japan Today, the large piece of rocket debris is expected to hit the moon at an estimated 5,400 mph or 8,690 kph, which is seven times the speed of sound.
While a piece of debris hitting the moon might seem like an inconsequential event for most people, scientists and astronomers are keeping a close eye on it because this will be one of the few times that an object will impact the moon while being observed. NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter and South Korea’s Danuri lunar orbiter will take before-and-after photos of the impact site, while the latter will also fly close to the stricken SpaceX rocket a few minutes before it begins its final descent.
NASA has previously deliberately crashed objects on the moon — it did this with sections of the Saturn V rocket and discarded Lunar Landers to conduct seismic experiments during the Apollo missions in the 70s. It repeated the experiment in 2009 with its LCROSS mission, where it crashed the probe near the south pole of the moon in search of ice.
What interests researchers this time is how the impact will affect the surface of the moon, which is expected to deliver energy that’s equal to about three tons of TNT. Even though this might seem like a huge amount of energy, we likely cannot see the actual crash from Earth. But because the moon does not have wind or an atmosphere, the ejected material could stretch for miles and be visible on telescopes.
“The gravity on the moon is low and there is no wind to blow the dust away,” said Benjamin Fernando of the Los Alamos National Laboratory. “Part of the reason for our interest in this event is to figure out how much of a hazard debris impacts pose to future astronauts.”
Space debris is not a major concern for the moon as it is for our planet at the moment, but this might change in the near future. As the U.S. and China are locked in a space race to see who will be the first one to land on people on the moon again after more than half a century, there will soon come a time when operators cannot just leave their rocket debris in an orbital decay, lest it come crashing down on their settlements and data centers.

articles.title: Sunscreen, beach towel... security camera? Smart home expert Chris Price builds the ultimate tech setup to protect your property while you're on vacation
articles.text:
Is your home safe this summer? Security tech expert Chris Price shows how to expand a single camera into a budget-friendly home defence setup for when you're away on vacation
Peace of mind on the beach
Planning a summer getaway but worried about leaving your house for a few weeks? While statistically you are more likely to suffer a break-in during the winter months when it’s much darker, summer also presents an ideal opportunity for burglars. Even if you're at home there are increased risks, especially if you leave your windows open to get some fresh air into the house during a heatwave.
Of course, there are basic steps you can take to reduce your risk such as asking a neighbor to take in your mail and packages, and making sure windows are closed when you go out. But technology can help big time too. What’s more, you don’t have to spend a fortune on all the gear. Whereas once you had to spend thousands on security cameras and PVRs (personal video recorders) that had to be professionally installed, now you can buy cameras and video doorbells for a fraction of the price that can be controlled easily via your smartphone.
Starting simple
The trick is to start simple. A good idea if you are going away for a long time is to have an indoor camera focused on the most vulnerable part of the house where a burglar is most likely to break in — such as a back door. I’ve got a Nest Cam IQ Indoor focused on my patio doors leading out to the garden. I like it because it can record when it hears sound (such as glass breaking) as well as motion.
However, there are other cheaper models available from companies such as Amazon-owned Blink and Ring as well as lesser-known, but popular, Chinese brands such as EZVIZ, Reolink and Aqara.
Focused on the front door I have a tiny Blink Mini 2K+ which also provides a chime for the Blink video doorbell so we can hear it ringing in the house. Usually, I switch the motion sensor off on the Blink Mini during the day because it’s triggered every time a family member opens the front door which can be a bit of a pain. However, when I go on holiday I switch the motion sensor on just in case.
One important consideration is how footage is stored — either locally on a MicroSD card or in the cloud. Personally, I prefer storing footage locally on an SD card, although the downside is that you will usually have to buy a card separately. The advantage of local storage is that not only is it generally more secure (there have been cases of servers being hacked and private security footage being leaked), it also often works out cheaper in the long term.
That’s because many home security companies will charge you a monthly subscription fee to store all your recorded footage and access advanced AI-driven features such as facial recognition and text descriptions of videos.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
While these features may be vaguely useful, especially if you have lots of people coming to the door, for the vast majority it’s probably not worth the monthly fee.
Let’s go outside
Obviously, no discussion of home security is complete without talking about outdoor cameras and video doorbells. Whether it’s summer or winter, these devices are invaluable when it comes to optimizing your home security set-up and helping to prevent burglary.
Choosing the type of outdoor camera you want is largely down to personal choice and the type of property you live in. Generally speaking, outdoor cameras should be mounted reasonably high on your property to give you a better view and to prevent theft.
Many offer a wide viewing angle of between 130 and 180 degrees, while some of the latest models, such as the latest IMOU AOV PT, are pan-and-tilt models that detect and track movement automatically.
Want a security camera to act as a deterrent to an opportunist burglar? Then it’s worth considering a device with a powerful built-in spotlight and loud siren. If there are two things that burglars hate more than anything else, they're excessive noise and light that draws attention to what they are up to. Reolink’s Solar Floodlight Cam covers both bases with twin spotlights either side of the camera and an integrated 110dB siren.
Going solar
Unlike indoor cameras, which usually plug into the mains, powering an outdoor camera is a little more challenging. Although some are designed to plug into the mains via a waterproof housing, most now rely on either disposable/rechargeable batteries and/or solar power. Indeed, solar-powered cameras, such as the Reolink Solar Floodlight Cam mentioned above, have become increasingly popular in the UK particularly as summers have got hotter and panels have become more efficient.
While many of the latest outdoor cameras comprise separate solar panels that need to be mounted separately and plugged into a USB-C socket on the camera, others such as the IMOU Cell 3C come with a solar panel built in. Chinese company Baseus even has an innovative solar-powered camera, the Baseus Security S2, that boasts an innovative rotating solar panel that moves as the sun moves in order to maximize power to the camera.
Deciding how to power your outdoor camera isn’t the only factor you need to consider either. You also need to think about the technology you are going to use to transmit video clips to your phone’s security camera app. While for indoor cameras this is usually WiFi, for outdoor devices getting a connection between the indoor router and outdoor camera can be more challenging — especially over distances of around 30m.
One option therefore, may be to buy a device that offers dual-connectivity, including Wi-Fi and cellular (usually 4G), such as the IMOU AOV PT or Eufy 4G LTE Cam S330.
Optimizing your setup
So you’ve got your outdoor camera. What next? Well, now begins the process of optimizing it for your security needs. Generally, most outdoor cameras are far too sensitive and record far more footage than you actually need to look at. As a result, you could find your entire time on holiday viewing footage of someone walking past your house, or a car whizzing by, instead of enjoying quality time away.
Not only is this highly annoying, it could really waste battery power — something that's both costly and time-consuming, especially if you have to climb up on a ladder to take the device down to recharge or change the batteries every couple of weeks.
Within the app, it’s therefore a good idea to set the motion detection zones so that the camera only records footage captured on your property and also reduce the sensitivity settings too so the camera isn’t recording too much footage. If you know you are going to be away for a set period of time then it’s probably a good idea to ensure the camera can detect motion 24/7, but when you are home you may want to use the menus so it only records at time of the day when you know family members or flat mates aren’t going to be entering or leaving the property (such as night time).
When it comes to video quality, most outdoor cameras now offer at least 1080p video quality. However, some such as the Baseus Security S2 and the Reolink Altas PT Ultra, offer stunning 4K picture quality. While this is great, especially if you want to zoom in on close ups of a potential suspect, most of the time it’s probably unnecessary. By reducing video quality you will be able to store more footage on the SD card/in the cloud and not consume as much power either.
For night-time monitoring, standard infra-red (IR) night vision provides clear monochrome visibility in total darkness while a colour night-vision option uses advanced low-light sensors or built-in LED spotlights to capture colour details after dark.
Video doorbells — it’s good to talk
Think someone may be intruding on your property while you’re not around? All security cameras that I’ve ever tested (probably over 50 now) feature two-way audio so you can, if you so wish, talk directly to the intruder to tell him or her to get off your land. And they can also talk back to you, of course, using the built-in microphone.
Some of the latest models even generate automated messages or use different voices so the person doesn’t actually know who they are talking to (for example the Aqara G100 indoor/outdoor security camera lets you turn your voice into that of a robot or clown.) It’s a feature that some women and teens in particular might find reassuring, especially if they don’t want a man to think they are at home by themselves — though I can’t help thinking of Kevin McCallister in the film Home Alone.
Essentially video doorbells take the technology one step further by enabling you to speak directly to people who press the button, even if you are sitting on beach sipping a strawberry daiquiri on your summer vacation (as with the G100, Aqara’s G410 Doorbell Camera Hub also allows you to disguise your voice). Invented by Ring’s founder Jamie Siminoff back in 2013, video doorbells have really taken off in the last few years with most home security manufacturers now producing models.
Usefully, not only do video doorbells enable you to talk to whoever comes to the door as if you were at home, they can also be set up to detect and record nearby movement just like standard outdoor security cameras. The only real difference is that, whereas outdoor security cameras often have a wide viewing angle and wide aspect ratio, video doorbells tend to offer a much squarer field of view — often 1:1 — so you can see whoever is at the door more clearly.
Advanced functionality
For those looking to replace their traditional doorbell, video doorbells are a great solution. With many models, it’s even possible to use existing doorbell wiring to power them, rather than having to rely on disposable or rechargeable batteries. Many come with separate plug-in chimes so you can hear the doorbell clearly inside the house with a choice of customizable ‘ringtones’, ranging from classical music to Christmas carols.

That’s not to say that video doorbells are the perfect security solution for everyone. They’re not. Often, I’ve found there is quite a lag when you are talking to someone and if you live on a busy street it can be difficult to hear what they are saying. To counter this, some models, including those from Ring, enable you to play automated responses to the visitor, a bit like an old-fashioned answerphone — for example, ‘please leave the parcel outside’ or ‘call back in an hour’s time’.
Another issue is that with subscription services such as Ring Pro you can spend up to $19.99 / £15.99 a month on premium features such as person, package and vehicle alerts, video descriptions and 180 day video playback. At least with a Blink video doorbell it’s possible to store clips on the Blink Sync Module 2 hub using a separate USB drive while the TP Link Tapo D235 is one of the few doorbells with integrated MicroSD storage (it also offers free AI smart detection to distinguish between vehicles, pets and people).
Complete security solutions
Looking for a more advanced security solution for when you go away over the summer? Most manufacturers will allow you to view several cameras via their app. However, if you want to put different types of security devices together — such as locks, lights and a burglar alarm — then you will need a more advanced setup.
For example, one advantage of the Aqara G410 video doorbell is that it’s actually a fully-fledged smart home hub with a built-in Matter bridge and Thread border router that can be used as part of a smart home ecosystem such as Apple HomeKit, Google Home, Amazon Alexa and Smart Things.
Owned by Amazon, Ring products including cameras, video doorbells and burglar alarms can easily be controlled using Alexa routines with footage viewable via Echo Show devices. Furthermore, Ring Alarm also supports certified third-party products via the encrypted Z-Wave network, including smart locks from Yale, Schlage and Kwikset. This means you can lock/unlock doors, manage guest PIN codes and trigger automated security routines (such as arming the alarm when the door is locked) all inside the Ring app.
Securing your home for summer
With the summer holiday season well and truly upon us, and houses left empty as we down tools for a well needed break, now is the time to think about securing your home. While traditional precautions — such as securing windows, clearing letterboxes and locking away garden tools (including ladders) — remain essential precautions, modern technology can help too.
Protecting your home against burglary needn’t cost the earth either. You can now buy indoor cameras focused on vulnerable parts of the house for less than $70 / £50 while most outdoor cameras and video doorbells cost between $120 / £100 and $250 / £200. And while subscription charges do push up prices, often these aren’t necessary — especially if you can store footage locally on an SD card or USB drive.
Ultimately, combining the latest tech solutions with solid physical security will give you the peace of mind needed for you to truly unwind, ensuring your home remains a well-guarded fortress while you enjoy your break.

articles.title: Ya conocemos otra función estrella de las gafas inteligentes de Apple. Y sí, es otra cosa que llegaría tarde a Europa (o nunca)
articles.text:
Parece que Apple tiene un plan para hacer aún más atractivas sus próximas gafas inteligentes. Todo apunta a que no se presentarán oficialmente hasta el 2027, pero todas las miradas ya están puestas sobre la compañía y la división encargada de sacarlas adelante. Tanto foco está haciendo que algunos detalles salgan a la luz, como la necesidad de fichar un nuevo talento dentro del departamento Vision. ¿Para qué? Ahí está la clave: esta búsqueda nos permite pensar que las gafas inteligentes de Apple van a ser más interesantes de lo esperado.
De hecho, Mark Gurman no se ha andado con rodeos: afirma que las gafas inteligentes de Apple van a tener una nueva característica que no se espera y que, además, no está presente en ningún otro modelo actualmente. Y, poniendo sobre la mesa la nueva vacante de Apple, hay pocas formas de traducirlo.
Todo apunta a que las gafas inteligentes de Apple van a contar con opciones avanzadas de monitorización de ejercicio y salud. No se quedarán solo en la IA, la grabación y la escucha de música: la compañía podría incluir varios sensores para permitirte dejar a un lado otros gadgets como el Apple Watch.
Apple ha comentado que necesita fichar a una persona para "definir el futuro de las experiencias de salud, bienestar y fitness en el ámbito de los productos Vision". Y, para quien no lo sepa todavía, Vision es el sistema operativo y la interfaz de las actuales gafas inteligentes de realidad aumentada de Apple, las Vision Pro.
Las gafas inteligentes de Apple podrían ser más interesantes de lo esperado
Desde que sabemos que las gafas inteligentes de Apple están sobre la mesa, hay varias características prácticamente confirmadas: la posibilidad de grabar en POV, la reproducción de contenido a través de sus altavoces integrados y el uso de Siri AI a través de la voz y el contexto visual. Ahora se suma otra gran función a la ecuación: la salud.
Parece bastante viable que las gafas inteligentes de Apple incluyan sensores relacionados con la salud, como un monitor de frecuencia cardiaca para medir las pulsaciones al hacer deporte o giroscopios extra para monitorizar tus movimientos con precisión. Todo, con el objetivo de hacer que este gadget sea un aliado a la hora de hacer deporte, medir tus pasos diarios o, incluso, convertirse en una fuente de información sobre tu salud.
Las opciones son casi infinitas gracias a su naturaleza. Las gafas inteligentes de Apple no solo podrían medir tus pulsaciones, sino también utilizar la cámara para "ver" cómo realizas un ejercicio y contrastarlo con Siri AI para corregirte. Sumar la visión a la ecuación de la salud es sumamente interesante, porque abre un mundo de posibilidades, como la opción de registrar tus comidas de forma automática, por ejemplo.
Ahora bien, todos estos planes llegan un poco tarde. A pesar de que todavía quedaría más de un año para conocer las gafas inteligentes de Apple, estar buscando un perfil a estas alturas de la película nos permite pensar que la compañía podría estar planteando incluir la salud más adelante o en una segunda generación. Por ahora, toca esperar pacientemente.

articles.title: A Marc Benioff-backed startup thinks AI can solve the AI deployment problem | TechCrunch
articles.text:
It’s so hard for big businesses to get AI tools working reliably that whole new organizations of forward-deployed engineers or FDEs— specialists who drop into a company to get its AI systems up and running — are springing up to help them.
“AI, paradoxically, increases the demand for professional services,” says Efrat Rapoport, a former Salesforce executive whose new company, June, emerged from stealth Monday morning. “The industry’s answer to AI implementation is, ‘let’s hire more and more and more people.”
Rapoport and her three cofounders — Ohad Hen, Barak Goldstein, and Idan Tsitiat — have a different idea about how to bring AI into broader use. To pursue it, the company raised $20 million in pre-seed funding led by Marc Benioff’s Time Ventures, with additional backing from tech luminaries like Michael Dell, Aaron Levie and George Kurtz. The company declined to share its valuation.
The four founders previously started Bonobo AI, a pre-transformer language model company that launched a voice-to-text service in 2017. Bonobo AI was snapped up two years later by Salesforce, and the team worked for several years on the tech giant’s AI initiatives before setting out on their own again after watching customers struggle to bring AI into their existing platforms.
Their potential was clear enough to their investors, Rapoport says, that “we didn’t even have a deck for this raise.”
While the so-called SaaSpocalypse has software firms fearing that AI might replace them, thus far no one is vibe-coding a CRM for a Fortune 500 company. Any AI model brought into a corporate setting still has to work with Salesforce, ServiceNow, DataBricks, Workday, or any of a dozen other data-management platforms.
“Before AI can create value, someone has to deal with legacy systems,” Rapoport says. “You have fragmented data across these platforms. You have complex workflows. You have years of technical debt.”
Building an agent template is the easy part, she says. The hard part is getting it to work with the mess underneath. “How does an agent know how to operate when you have 10 duplicate [database] fields that say the same thing, and different teams are using them?”
June’s platform scans a company’s existing systems to understand its business processes, find bottlenecks, and then build more optimized, agent-powered processes to replace them, automatically notifying teams through the company’s comms channels.
“We give you the full roadmap automatically of what needs to happen step by step for you to actually implement this agent successfully in an enterprise environment, which is often very complex,” Rapoport said. “We give you a step by step guide. ‘Remove these duplicates. Connect to this data source.’ And then you click on ‘build’ on each task, and June starts building it for you in the organization.”
Paul Akinmade, chief strategy officer at CMG, a major U.S. mortgage lender, moved his company’s software engineering over to Claude Code quickly, but hit roadblocks trying to integrate it with Salesforce. That was a problem since he’d promised at Salesforce’s annual conference the year before that he’d return with 100 agents running, and it wasn’t looking like he’d hit that target. 
Akinmade says his team spent weeks hitting a wall — meeting with architects, talking to forward-deployed engineers, consulting everybody they could — without making progress. June changed that, he says, giving his team a clear view of where to deploy agents and letting them do so safely, even before the official kickoff call between the two companies
Rapoport sees June as a tool that complements FDEs and consultants, but her customers may be drawn to it for the opposite reason: it lets them avoid FDEs altogether.
When Akinmade was first considering piloting the tool at CMG, he says he told her: “If your product requires FDEs, I don’t want your product. I’ve already I’ve already done that and I’m getting annoyed by it. I don’t want a black box. I don’t want something only certain people can figure out. I want an easy-to-use tool.”
Evidently, June cleared the bar.

articles.title: Celebrating the AI Act delay? The EU AI Act’s chatbot and content rules apply this week
articles.text:
Celebrating the AI Act delay? The EU AI Act’s chatbot and content rules apply this week
While high-risk AI penalties are on hold, Article 50 is now in effect, and SMEs need to be ready
If your business celebrated the European Union’s (EU) delay of high-risk AI penalties, don't open the champagne just yet. On August 2, 2026, Article 50 of the EU AI Act goes live, bringing new transparency requirements for the AI tools businesses already rely on. While backend compliance demands have been delayed, chatbots, AI generators, and synthetic media systems are now in the spotlight.
The AI Act delays may have dominated headlines, but Article 50 never stopped moving. The European Commission has now finalized the transparency guidelines businesses need to follow, giving regulators a clear framework to enforce consumer disclosure rules starting this weekend.
Think the EU AI Act only targets big tech? Think again. Small or medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) serving European users are also in scope, wherever they operate. The age of invisible AI is ending, and businesses that hide automated interactions may find themselves under significant regulatory scrutiny before the business week even begins.
Who is caught in the net? Providers vs deployers
To navigate the EU AI Act without getting lost in legal jargon, businesses must first understand which role they fall under. The framework separates organizations into two categories: Providers and Deployers. Mixing up these definitions is the fastest way to accidentally skip a critical regulatory step or waste time trying to solve compliance issues that aren't actually your responsibility.
If your company builds AI models from scratch, significantly modifies open-source systems, or white-labels a third-party AI tool to sell under your own brand name, you are a Provider under the EU AI Act. That puts the technical burden on your business, from building transparency infrastructure to embedding machine-readable watermarks into AI-generated text, images, and videos.
For most SMEs, however, the second category applies: Deployers. If you are a small business that simply plugs an off-the-shelf AI widget into your website to handle customer service tickets, or uses AI tools to create marketing content, you are deploying AI. Thankfully, your responsibility isn't to invent deep-tech watermarking protocols but to double-check that people interacting with your systems are notified that they are dealing with an algorithm rather than a human employee.
The AI Act timeline: What was delayed vs what is due now
When the EU delayed major AI Act deadlines, businesses were quick to assume they had more time. The May 2026 "Digital Omnibus" amendment formally rolled back the compliance deadlines for complex AI architectures, leading many burned-out business owners to assume the entire rulebook had been kicked down the road.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
Unfortunately, that was a serious misunderstanding of the changes. The extensions only apply to standalone, high-risk frameworks, such as automated resume screening, biometric identity verification, and AI-powered credit scoring tools. Because these deep enterprise tools require massive infrastructure overhauls and independent third-party audits, the EU simply gave businesses a longer runway until late 2027 and 2028 to prepare.
Basic consumer transparency, however, received no free pass. The European Commission made it clear that protecting everyday users from digital deception could not be delayed. As a result, Article 50 moves forward on schedule, separate from the postponed systemic deadlines. To guide businesses through this transition, the EU has established the Code of Practice on Transparency of AI-generated Content as the benchmark for compliance.
Article 50 and the four pillars of AI transparency
If your business utilizes AI to interact with customers or create content, Article 50 is now part of your operating reality. The EU has broken down its transparency rules into four core pillars, aiming to remove the mystery around automated systems without slowing down innovation.
For SMEs, the era of set-it-and-forget-it AI is firmly over. Depending on how your business uses generative tools, you are now legally required to update user interfaces, verify compliance from software vendors, or change how AI-generated content is published.
AI chatbot transparency rules
The first pillar is the “Human-AI Interaction” rule, and it targets the conversational bots handling your customer service, lead generation, or basic troubleshooting. Under the new guidelines, you can no longer trick a consumer into thinking they are chatting with a human employee when they are actually interacting with a large language model (LLM) script.
Starting this week, deployers must stop hiding AI behind a human-looking interface. Crucially, users need a clear notification that they are interacting with an AI system before the conversation starts, not a disclaimer buried in a wall of legal text. For SMEs using AI customer support, that means updating chat interfaces immediately to include an undeniable "I am an AI assistant" disclaimer.
Synthetic media watermarking
The second pillar shifts the technical burden onto the builders of generative AI tools. If your business creates or distributes software that generates synthetic text, audio, images, or video, you must embed machine-readable digital watermarks into the assets those tools produce.
The purpose of these markers is to help other software, like social media platforms or verification services, automatically detect that a piece of media was created by an AI. While existing providers have limited time to implement this infrastructure, any new generative AI tools launched after this week must include watermarking from day one.
Labeling AI-generated content
While watermarking happens behind the scenes, the third pillar requires clear labeling on the surface of the content itself. This rule specifically targets what the EU defines as deepfakes and synthetic output that could influence public understanding. If your marketing team uses AI to create realistic images, videos, or audio that could be mistaken for real people or events, you must slap a clear “AI-generated” warning label on them.
This responsibility falls on the businesses publishing the content. So, if you publish an AI-generated image of a realistic crowd for a promotional campaign, or use an AI-voiced avatar in a public video, it must also feature an overlay or disclaimer stating that it has been artificially generated or manipulated. The only exception here is obvious artistic, satirical, or fictional content, but transparency is still the safest bet.
Emotion recognition rules
The final, and perhaps most legally sensitive, pillar targets biometric and emotion-recognition systems. If your SME utilizes software to detect emotional states, interpret facial expressions, or classify individuals based on biometric data, you must proceed with extreme caution.
The new rules require businesses to explicitly inform users whenever they are exposed to emotion recognition or biometric profiling systems. For instance, if you use an AI-driven video interviewing tool to analyze a candidate's body language, or a retail system checking customer reactions, you must secure clear user consent before the software starts collecting this type of sensitive data. Psychological and physiological tracking can no longer happen behind closed doors.
The AI Act’s hidden deadline split
Like with any major regulatory rollout, the devil is always in the details. For SMEs, the EU AI Act brings a mix of breathing room and immediate pressure. Understanding which deadlines moved (and which did not) is the only way to avoid a costly compliance mistake.
The good news for software creators and IT departments is what experts call the grandfather clause. If your generative AI model was already legally available on the market before August 2, 2026, the EU provides a four-month technical runway, which moves mandatory machine-readable watermarking requirements to December 2, 2026. This extension gives development teams a much-needed time to update systems, test metadata workflows, and prepare for compliance.
However, relying too much on this buffer is where SMEs fall into a terrible, zero-day trap. The four-month grace period applies only to the technical back-end watermarking of existing AI tools, and it doesn’t cover chatbots, public disclosures, or newly launched software.
If you’re launching a brand new AI writing tool or chatbot after this week, there is no ramp-up window. Similarly, user disclaimers for deepfakes and interactive chatbots must be active immediately on day one. Without clear AI notices on customer-facing systems, your business becomes non-compliant the moment the deadline passes.
How to comply before Monday morning
If your business is staring down the barrel of the August 2nd deadline, the answer is not panic but preparation. Since there is no single EU registry for AI tools, compliance starts with something much simpler: making your AI use visible, documented, and transparent.
You do not need to rebuild your software stack over the weekend, but you do need to secure your customer-facing AI touchpoints. Here are four steps to take before Monday:
- Map your stealth AI usage: Audit your teams for untracked software, plugins, and automated systems creating customer-facing content.
- Kill the invisible chatbots: Update AI chat tools with a clear upfront notice telling users they are interacting with an AI assistant.
- Verify software vendor compliance: Get written confirmation of compliance and ask how providers handle machine-readable watermarks.
- Document your paper trail: Log every AI update, vendor conversation, and internal policy change for future reviews.
Turning compliance into trust
For many businesses, Article 50 feels like a new burden, but for smart SMEs, it is a chance to build trust. As users grow more skeptical of hidden AI, businesses that are transparent about how they use automation can stand out from the crowd.
Compliance is no longer another box to check to avoid penalties but a powerful indicator of integrity that can set your brand apart in the new age of AI.
Sead is a seasoned freelance journalist based in Sarajevo, Bosnia and Herzegovina. He writes about IT (cloud, IoT, 5G, VPN) and cybersecurity (ransomware, data breaches, laws and regulations). In his career, spanning more than a decade, he’s written for numerous media outlets, including Al Jazeera Balkans. He’s also held several modules on content writing for Represent Communications.

articles.title: « On est allé trop loin » : Mercedes admet les limites du tout-tactile et annonce le retour des boutons physiques
articles.text:
Dans la course aux technologies embarquées, Mercedes fait partie des constructeurs les plus audacieux avec son système « MBUX Superscreen/Hyperscreen ». Une enfilade d’affichage, voire une dalle monumentale unique qui peut atteindre 1 mètre de largeur sur certains modèles, symbolise l’apogée de la numérisation des cockpits.
Pourtant, l’enthousiasme pour ces interfaces intégralement tactiles s’est heurté à la réalité du quotidien : des manipulations parfois complexes en roulant et une frustration grandissante chez une partie de la clientèle. Dans une interview publiée le 31 juillet 2026 par Autocar, le patron de Mercedes reconnaît avoir été « trop loin » en retirant bon nombre de boutons physiques au profit des affichages.
Trouver la bonne recette à bord des Mercedes
Conscient de ces réserves, le patron du constructeur allemand, Ola Källenius, a insisté sur l’importance du travail sur l’interface utilisateur. Lors d’échanges réguliers avec ses équipes d’ingénieurs, le dirigeant résume l’exigence d’ergonomie par une contrainte : « cela doit être suffisamment intuitif pour être manipulé sans hésitation aussi bien par un enfant de cinq ans que par un membre du conseil d’administration ».
Une logique implacable, qui n’est pourtant pas vraiment appliquée à l’heure actuelle. Dans notre essai de la nouvelle CLA électrique, nous nous sommes heurtés à une ergonomie discutable, entre manque de boutons physiques justement, et commandes tactiles moins naturelles.
Ola Källenius concède ouvertement que le secteur automobile a probablement franchi un seuil excessif en supprimant massivement les boutons classiques. Il admet que l’industrie s’est parfois laissé porter par la « technologie pour la technologie », quitte à nuire légèrement à l’expérience utilisateur.
Le retour des boutons physiques chez Mercedes
Interrogé sur l’évolution future des cockpits, le directeur écarte l’idée d’un recul de la taille des écrans. En revanche, il affirme que le secteur a atteint ce qu’il qualifie de « point bas du bouton ».
L’objectif n’est donc pas de faire machine arrière sur le numérique, mais plutôt d’opérer un rééquilibrage plus pragmatique : « désormais, vous nous verrez réintroduire les boutons les plus pratiques », annonce Ola Källenius. Le patron n’a pas décrit précisément quel contrôle allait se (re)faire par des boutons. À l’heure actuelle, les réglages de climatisation ou le changement de musique/station de radio se font par exemple uniquement via l’écran.

articles.title: Outcome-first AI: redesigning enterprise service delivery at scale
articles.text:
Outcome-first AI: redesigning enterprise service delivery at scale
At DevSparks Bengaluru 2026, EY GDS partner Tanu Garg said AI is not a productivity add-on, but a complete redesign of how services get built and delivered.
When EY GDS Partner Tanu Garg took the stage at DevSparks Bengaluru 2026, she challenged one of the most common assumptions about enterprise AI: that its primary role is automation.
“Artificial Intelligence (AI) is not about making existing processes faster. It is about rewiring how enterprises deliver value.”
For Garg, who leads AI Service Delivery Transformation at EY Global Delivery Services, the distinction matters. While productivity and efficiency remain important outcomes, she believes AI is also reshaping how work is designed, decisions are made, and value is delivered across the enterprise.
Historically, service delivery was built around human capacity and linear workflows. Today, human expertise, digital agents and intelligent workflows are beginning to operate together, changing how work moves across teams and how decisions are made.
According to Garg, organizations are increasingly examining how workflows, operating models and decision-making processes need to evolve as AI becomes part of everyday operations.
From AI adoption to AI-native operating models
A recurring theme in Garg's session was that many AI programs begin with isolated use cases that improve efficiency but leave underlying processes unchanged.
Garg highlighted three areas she believes are critical for enterprise AI transformation.
The first is process redesign around outcomes rather than activities. She referenced EY.ai Value Blueprints as an approach to help organizations examine workflows end-to-end, identify bottlenecks and decision points, and rethink how outcomes are produced.
“The goal is not to optimize a broken process. The goal is to reimagine how the outcome is achieved.”
Garg said that many organizations struggle because AI is often applied to existing ways of working without questioning whether they remain fit for purpose. The opportunity lies in redesigning workflows and decision-making for an AI-enabled environment.
The second is scaling AI beyond pilots into production environments. While many organizations have experimented with AI over the past two years, moving successful use cases into day-to-day operations remains a challenge.
Garg pointed to the AI Engine Room as an example of how organizations can move AI initiatives from experimentation into business operations through reusable assets and governance mechanisms.
“We see the Engine Room as a production capability, not an experimentation environment.”
She also emphasized that as AI becomes more widely available, context is becoming a critical differentiator.
“The next frontier is context."
In her view, reliable outcomes depend on more than model performance. Industry knowledge, enterprise data, governance requirements and business context all play an important role.
The third area centers on workforce readiness, governance and responsible adoption. Garg stressed that trust, explainability and accountability should be embedded into AI programs from the beginning rather than treated as compliance requirements added later.
“The success of AI transformation is not determined by technology adoption. It is determined by how effectively organizations enable people, governance and trust alongside technology.”
Together, these themes reflected a consistent message from Garg's session: the challenge for many organizations is no longer experimenting with AI, but embedding it into the way work gets done.
Measuring value realization, not effort
Another theme from the session was how AI is changing the way organizations measure performance.
Traditional service delivery models have often measured performance through hours worked, resources deployed and activities completed. Garg argued that AI is beginning to change that equation.
As routine work becomes increasingly automated, organizations are placing greater emphasis on outcomes such as speed to market, quality improvement, process simplification, workforce effectiveness, and revenue growth.
To support this shift, Garg referenced the EY Value Realization framework, which links transformation initiatives to measurable business outcomes.
“You monetize impact, not effort.”
According to Garg, this shift influences more than delivery metrics. It also affects how organizations prioritize investments, assess transformation programs and evaluate returns from AI initiatives.
How AI changes workforce roles
Garg was equally clear that AI is changing the role of people.
As AI takes on more routine activities, roles across engineering, architecture, product management and risk are increasingly shifting toward oversight, orchestration and decision-making.
To illustrate the point, Garg shared an AI-enabled product development example in which a car booking application for a US travel management firm was delivered in three and a half weeks with a six-person team. A traditional approach would have required roughly 12 professionals over four months. The example demonstrates how teams can operate differently when AI becomes embedded into the delivery process across requirements, design, coding and testing activities.
A second example drew on EY.ai for Risk, where AI supports routine activities while complex business, risk and compliance decisions remain under human oversight, helping maintain accountability and trust. The solution was co-designed with Gen Z workforce of EY and built on a continuous cycle of training, human validation and regulatory requirements, reinforcing the importance of transparency and human judgment in AI-enabled decision-making.
The example reflected a broader theme from Garg's session: as AI adoption scales, governance, explainability and human oversight become increasingly important.
The next phase: outcome-first AI
Garg's session reflected a broader shift taking place across enterprise AI conversations.
Early adoption focused on tools, pilots and productivity gains. Organizations are now examining how AI changes the way work is designed, decisions are made and value is delivered.
Her central message was that AI delivers meaningful business value when it becomes part of the operating model rather than an isolated technology initiative.
As enterprises move beyond experimentation, the challenge is increasingly about scaling AI in ways that improve business outcomes while maintaining trust, accountability and human judgment.

articles.title: Cuando el fuego crea sus propias tormentas: el aterrador auge de los pirocumulonimbos y su impacto "volcánico"
articles.text:
Este verano estamos viviendo una cadena de incendios forestales que sin duda va a pasar a la historia por su gran magnitud y por las imágenes extremas y sin precedentes que nos han dejado. Francia ha sido uno de los países más afectados, junto a España, y donde se ha visto un fenómeno meteorológico que parece sacado de una película de catástrofes: nubes de tormenta masivas que no nacen del ciclo natural del clima, sino del calor extremo de las llamas.
Algo conocido. Con este fenómeno no estamos hablando de simples columnas de humo, sino que se trata de un fenómeno climático con entidad propia que fascina y preocupa a la comunidad científica y que es conocido como los pirocumulonimbos. Y lejos de ser una rareza anecdótica, están alterando nuestra atmósfera a una escala que apenas estamos empezando a comprender.
Los pirocumulonimbos. Si acudimos a las referencias estándar en meteorología, como el glosario oficial de la Sociedad Meteorológica Americana, encontramos que los pirocumulonimbos son, en esencia, tormentas generadas por incendios.
Esto quiere decir que cuando un fuego es lo suficientemente masivo e intenso, genera corrientes ascendentes de aire extremadamente caliente. Este aire arrastra consigo vapor de agua, cenizas y partículas de humo hacia lo alto de la atmósfera y, al alcanzar las capas más frías, el vapor se condensa formando una inmensa nube convectiva. El resultado es una tormenta perfecta que puede generar rayos (lo que a su vez provoca nuevos focos de incendio) e inyectar grandes cantidades de humo directamente en la alta troposfera y la baja estratosfera.
Como un volcán. Durante mucho tiempo, la magnitud de estas tormentas de fuego fue subestimada. Pero a partir del año 2010 la ciencia comenzó a destapar todo lo que no conocíamos de estos fenómenos gracias a la detección por satélite. Aquí un estudio de 2018 apuntó que las tormentas provocaron una inyección estratosférica de humo similar a la de un volcán. Se calcula que un gran pirocumulonimbo puede inyectar entre 0,1 y 0,3 teragramos de aerosoles de humo en la estratósfera, un orden de magnitud muy superior a lo que se estimaba en el pasado.
Lo hemos vivido. Uno de los ejemplos más devastadores que hemos visto en nuestra historia como sociedad lo tenemos en el "verano negro" que vivió Australia hace seis años. Aquí quedó documentada la existencia de 38 pirocumolonimbos que produjeron inyecciones estratosféricas masivas, alterando las condiciones atmosféricas a nivel global.
Tenemos que entenderlo. Con el cambio climático actuando como telón de fondo y propiciando perfiles atmosféricos cada vez más favorables para su formación, agencias como la NASA y el Laboratorio de Investigación Naval de EEUU se han puesto en marcha.
Actualmente, existen campañas de investigación punteras para cazar y entender a estos gigantes, y aquí destaca el proyecto INSPYRE, que es una campaña de campo plurianual que busca cuantificar cómo se inician estas tormentas y cómo retroalimentan el comportamiento extremo del fuego.

articles.title: iPhone Air 2 : Apple aurait déjà prévu plusieurs améliorations pour corriger les défauts du premier
articles.text:
Après un premier modèle qui misait avant tout sur la finesse, Apple préparerait déjà une nouvelle version de son iPhone Air. Au programme : un appareil photo supplémentaire, une puce plus moderne et plusieurs évolutions attendues dès le premier trimestre 2027.
D’après l’analyste Jeff Pu, qui suit de près les activités du groupe pour GF Securities, la firme de Cupertino envisagerait de dévoiler l’iPhone Air 2 dès le premier trimestre de l’année. Un modèle qui ne se contenterait pas d’une simple mise à jour, puisqu’il intégrerait déjà cinq évolutions majeures par rapport à la génération actuelle.
Un deuxième capteur photo et une puce A20 Pro en 2 nm au programme
La photo devrait compter parmi les principales nouveautés du smartphone ultrafin d'Apple. L'iPhone Air 2 embarquerait un deuxième capteur de 48 mégapixels au dos, associé cette fois à un objectif ultra grand-angle. Il viendrait ainsi compléter le capteur Fusion déjà présent sur la première génération.
Le géant de Cupertino prévoirait également de réduire légèrement la taille de la Dynamic Island. L'évolution resterait donc assez discrète sur la face avant, d'autant que le smartphone conserverait son écran de 6,5 pouces et sa caméra frontale Center Stage de 18 mégapixels. La quantité de mémoire vive resterait elle aussi fixée à 12 Go.
La partie interne profiterait en revanche de plusieurs modifications. L'iPhone Air 2 pourrait intégrer une puce A20 Pro plus rapide et moins énergivore, fabriquée par TSMC avec un procédé de gravure en 2 nm. Le modèle actuel s'appuie pour sa part sur une A19 Pro gravée en 3 nm.
De nouvelles puces Apple pour le réseau et la 5G
La connectivité sans fil devrait également évoluer avec l'arrivée d'une deuxième génération de la puce réseau d'Apple. Le modèle actuel embarque la N1, qui prend notamment en charge le Wi-Fi 7 et le Bluetooth 6 et contribue au fonctionnement de services comme AirDrop et le partage de connexion.
De son côté, la 5G devrait enfin bénéficier d'une nouvelle puce C2, appelée à succéder au modem C1X de l'actuel modèle. La marque à la pomme présente déjà ce dernier comme le modem le plus économe en énergie jamais intégré à un iPhone.
Selon les différents bruits de couloir, l'iPhone Air 2 devrait être présenté aux côtés de l'iPhone 18 et de l'iPhone 18e au printemps 2027. Apple aurait prévu une commercialisation différée pour les modèles haut de gamme, avec les iPhone 18 Pro, 18 Pro Max et le modèle pliant surnommé iPhone Ultra attendus quant à eux dès septembre.

articles.title: Managed IT And Helpdesk Support For Everyday Efficiency - Tech Guide
articles.text:
The Importance of Managed IT Services in Modern Business
In today’s fast-paced business environment, technology is the backbone that supports daily operations and strategic growth. For many companies, managing IT infrastructure internally can be both complex and costly. This is where managed IT services come into play, offering businesses a way to streamline operations, reduce downtime, and ensure their technology is always optimized for performance.
Managed IT services encompass a broad range of offerings, from maintaining hardware and software to proactive monitoring and cybersecurity. By outsourcing these responsibilities, businesses can free up internal resources and focus on their core competencies. According to a report by MarketsandMarkets, the global managed services market is expected to grow from $223 billion in 2020 to $329 billion by 2025, highlighting the increasing reliance on these services for operational efficiency.
Moreover, companies that adopt managed IT services often see improvements in system uptime and user satisfaction. In fact, 60% of organizations surveyed reported enhanced operational efficiency after partnering with managed service providers. This is largely because managed IT teams bring specialized expertise and tools that many internal IT departments may lack, especially in small to medium-sized businesses.
The benefits extend beyond just technical maintenance. Managed IT services provide strategic insights through data analytics and IT consulting, enabling businesses to make informed decisions about technology investments. This proactive approach helps organizations avoid costly downtime and align their IT infrastructure with long-term business goals.
Why Helpdesk Support Matters for Everyday Efficiency
One of the critical components of managed IT is helpdesk support. Effective helpdesk services act as the first line of defense against IT issues, providing quick resolutions and minimizing disruptions. A responsive helpdesk can significantly boost employee productivity by reducing downtime caused by technical problems.

Helpdesk support is not just about fixing immediate problems; it also plays a proactive role in identifying recurring issues and recommending system improvements. This proactive approach helps prevent future disruptions and contributes to a smoother IT environment. According to a study by HDI, organizations with strong help desk support experience 50% faster problem resolution times and 40% higher end-user satisfaction.
Additionally, helpdesk teams often manage user access, software licensing, and hardware upgrades, ensuring that employees have the tools they need to perform efficiently. Their role as a communication bridge between IT and end-users enhances transparency and trust within the organization.
The Benefits of Remote Helpdesk Solutions
Remote helpdesk support has become increasingly popular, especially with the rise of remote workforces. Remote helpdesk services enable IT professionals to diagnose and fix problems without the need for on-site visits, saving time and reducing operational costs.
A good example is the remote helpdesk by MC Services, which offers comprehensive support tailored to businesses of all sizes. Remote helpdesk services not only speed up issue resolution but also provide scalability. As companies grow or face fluctuating demand, remote teams can adapt quickly without the overhead of expanding in-house IT departments.
Statistically, businesses using remote IT support report a 25% reduction in downtime and a 30% improvement in issue resolution times. These improvements translate directly into cost savings and enhanced employee satisfaction. Furthermore, remote helpdesk services facilitate quicker deployment of software updates and security patches, which are critical in maintaining system integrity and compliance.
The rise of cloud computing and virtualization technologies has further amplified the effectiveness of remote helpdesk support. IT teams can remotely access servers, desktops, and applications to troubleshoot issues in real-time, minimizing delays and avoiding productivity losses. This flexibility is particularly beneficial for companies with distributed workforces or multiple office locations.
Remote helpdesk also supports seamless onboarding for new employees, enabling them to get the necessary IT setup and training without physical presence. This accelerates integration and reduces the burden on internal IT staff during peak hiring periods.
Enhancing Security Through Managed IT and Helpdesk Support
Security is a paramount concern for businesses handling sensitive data and critical operations. Managed IT providers and helpdesk teams play a vital role in maintaining robust cybersecurity protocols. They continuously monitor networks for threats, apply necessary patches, and educate employees on best practices.
By partnering with managed service providers, companies ensure they stay ahead of evolving cyber threats. The average cost of a data breach in 2023 was $4.45 million, underscoring the financial risks of inadequate IT security. Managed IT and helpdesk support help mitigate these risks by offering proactive security measures and rapid incident response.
Additionally, managed IT services often include compliance management, ensuring that businesses meet regulatory requirements such as GDPR, HIPAA, or PCI-DSS. This reduces the risk of penalties and enhances customer trust. For example, 70% of businesses that implemented managed IT security services reported fewer compliance issues and improved audit outcomes.
Helpdesk teams also contribute by providing end-user training on topics like phishing awareness and password management. Since human error is a leading cause of security breaches, this educational aspect is critical in building a strong security culture within organizations.
Furthermore, managed IT providers implement multi-layered security strategies, including firewalls, intrusion detection systems, and endpoint protection, which are continuously updated to address new vulnerabilities. Regular security audits and penetration testing are also part of comprehensive managed IT services, ensuring ongoing resilience against cyberattacks.
Improving Business Agility and Cost Management
Managed IT services and helpdesk support also contribute significantly to business agility. With expert teams handling IT infrastructure, companies can quickly adopt new technologies and scale their operations without the delays associated with internal resource constraints.
Additionally, cost management becomes more predictable. Rather than facing unexpected expenses for emergency IT fixes or hardware failures, businesses benefit from fixed monthly fees and transparent service agreements. This financial predictability supports better budgeting and resource allocation, essential for sustainable growth.
According to a Deloitte survey, companies leveraging managed IT services reduced their IT operational costs by an average of 20%, while also improving service quality and innovation capacity. This balance of cost efficiency and enhanced service delivery enables organizations to invest more confidently in strategic initiatives.
Business agility is further supported by the ability of managed IT providers to offer scalable solutions, including cloud migrations, disaster recovery, and data backup services. These capabilities ensure that companies can respond swiftly to market changes or unexpected disruptions, maintaining continuity and competitive advantage.
Moreover, managed IT services enable faster deployment of new applications and infrastructure upgrades, which can be crucial in gaining a competitive edge. The flexibility to scale IT resources up or down based on demand also helps avoid overprovisioning and reduces wasteful spending.
Choosing the Right Managed IT and Helpdesk Partner
Selecting the right managed IT and helpdesk provider is crucial for maximizing the benefits of these services. Factors to consider include the provider’s expertise, responsiveness, scalability, and commitment to security.
Organizations should look for partners who offer personalized support tailored to their unique needs and industries. Checking customer testimonials, service level agreements, and response times can provide valuable insights. It is also important to assess the provider’s technology stack and certifications to ensure alignment with your business objectives.
A trusted partner will not only resolve issues but also act as a strategic advisor, helping businesses leverage technology to drive innovation and growth. This collaborative approach fosters long-term relationships and continuous improvement.
Additionally, transparency in communication and reporting is essential. Providers should offer clear metrics on performance, security incidents, and system health, enabling businesses to track the value delivered and make informed decisions.
Conclusion
Managed IT and helpdesk support are no longer optional luxuries but essential components of a successful business strategy. They enhance everyday efficiency by reducing downtime, improving security, and enabling agility. As technology continues to evolve, partnering with experienced providers will empower businesses to stay competitive and focused on their core missions.
Investing in managed IT and helpdesk services is an investment in operational excellence and future-proof growth. By embracing these services, organizations can ensure that their technology infrastructure is resilient, secure, and aligned with their strategic goals, ultimately driving sustained success in an increasingly digital world.
With the right managed IT and help desk support, businesses can transform IT from a cost center into a strategic asset, enabling innovation, efficiency, and growth in every aspect of their operations.

articles.title: Le rejet de Windows 11 pousse Linux au-dessus des 10 % d'adoption pour la première fois de son histoire
articles.text:
Le rejet de Windows 11 pousse Linux au-dessus des 10 % d'adoption pour la première fois de son histoire
C'est un cap que Linux n'a jamais franchi jusque-là. En juillet 2026, Linux a atteint 10,65 % de parts de marché sur PC de bureau en Amérique du Nord selon Statcounter. Windows reste en tête mais dégringole à chaque mois.
En juin 2026, Statcounter mesurait Linux à 5,52 % de parts de marché dans la région. La part a donc doublé en un mois et approche les 12 % aux États-Unis. Sur ces deux mois, Windows est passé de 64,66 % à 57,63 %. Le désamour autour de Windows avantage donc Linux, pendant que macOS bouge à peine.
Linux passe au-dessus des 10 % d'adoption
Un détail explique une partie de ce doublement. En juin, la catégorie "Inconnu" de Statcounter pesait 9,24 % du trafic en Amérique du Nord. La catégorie regroupe les visites sans système d'exploitation identifié via des navigateurs et des outils qui masquent ces informations. En juillet, cette catégorie a nettement rétréci, au moment exact de la montée en puissance de Linux. Une meilleure identification du trafic expliquerait donc le bond fulgurant de Linux auprès des utilisateurs nord-américains.
Cloudflare confirme cette progression en expliquant que les requêtes de son réseau mondial place Linux à un niveau élevé sur les PC de bureau de la région. L'entreprise sépare le trafic humain probable du trafic automatisé, un détail décisif pour Linux, très présent sur les serveurs. Quand le tri est appliqué, la part tourne autour de 6 %. Les deux mesures reposent sur des données différentes et la conclusion reste la même, Linux grimpe.
Rappelons ce que ces chiffres mesurent. Le réseau de Statcounter dépasse le million de sites et cumule plus de 3 milliards de pages vues par mois. Depuis 2009, ces données mensuelles existent pour la région. Ces chiffres correspondent au trafic web et pas au nombre de PC installés. Une révision des données peut arriver pendant 45 jours. Personne ne peut affirmer qu'un PC de bureau sur dix tourne sous Linux en Amérique du Nord.
Les bugs de Windows 11 plombent sa popularité
Rappelons que la liste des reproches contre Windows est longue, très. Le 14 octobre 2025, Windows 10 a perdu son support, OS pourtant Ô combien populaire par rapport à son successeur, et les exigences matérielles de Windows 11 écartent des millions de PC.
S'ajoutent le compte Microsoft obligatoire pour utiliser Windows 11, les publicités du menu Démarrer ou encore l'IA ajouté au forceps. Copilot s'invite partout, du menu Démarrer à l'Explorateur de fichiers, pendant que sa part plafonne à 1 % sur le web selon SimilarWeb. Les mises à jour récentes ont ajouté leur lot de bugs et d'instabilité.
Le succès de Linux ne sort pas de nulle part, en dehors de ce rejet de Windows. L'installation de Linux est bien plus simple qu'avant et les grandes distributions se pilotent sans ligne de commande.
Le jeu vidéo a aussi participé à ce succès avec SteamOS basé sur Linux de Valve que l'on trouve sur ses Steam Deck et Steam Machine. Ces consoles prouvent aux sceptiques que le gaming confortable sur Linux est possible, parfois dans de meilleures conditions que sur Windows 11. En France, plusieurs administrations ont déjà remplacé l'OS de Microsoft par le logiciel libre.
En Inde, Linux dépassait 16 % dès juillet 2024 avec des PC vendus sans Windows pour réduire les prix. En Europe, les parts de Linux tournent entre 3 et 6 % selon les pays. L'Amérique du Nord est donc la première grande région au-dessus des 10 % chez Statcounter. Est-ce que la progression se poursuivra en août ? Réponse à la fin du mois.
