articles.title: ‘A lot of things are just dirty and need to be cleaned deeply’: I spent a day at a volunteer tech repair group learning how to fix tech from the experts, and found that some gadget repairs are easier than we think — maybe it's time to breathe life into your old hi-fi or headphones
articles.text:
'You can literally fix anything if you watch enough YouTube': I met with tech repair experts and campaigners to learn how to fix my broken gadgets — and why it's so important
How legislation, battery fires and community groups are changing the tech repair scene
Torn ear tips. Snapped charging case. Dented drivers. Like every other kind of gadget imaginable, the best headphones aren't built to last, and I'd wager that everyone reading this article has some skeletons (of old, ailing gadgets) in their (metaphorical) closet.
In fact, according to a European Union report, in 2024, 51% people kept their old smartphones even though they were no longer using them, and 34% were still holding onto their outdated laptops and tablets. We just don't know what to do with our old kit.
So, do you throw away your broken over-ear headphones and buy a new pair? Do you hunt down your nearest electronics recycling bank, or donate them to an organization which could use the parts? In recent years, the second-hand tech industry has boomed, with refurbishing and reselling sites such as Back Market and Refurbed ensuring that used gadgets get a second lease of life.
But too often, that first lease of life is all-too-easily abandoned. The tech you might be recycling — or consigning straight to landfill — might actually be easily repairable.
Per the BBC, a survey suggested that 7,000,000 wireless headphones (yes, seven-million) were thrown away in 2022, in the UK alone. And as we'll explore later, the majority of those may not have needed throwing away.
There's a simple truth. Gadget sellers are often loathe to admit it, worrying that repairing your own gadgets may affect their bottom line. And as we'll also soon learn, many companies seem to make repairs really quite difficult.
The thing is, your faulty gadget may be only a quick fix from working like new. From complicated pieces of kit such as AV machines and computers, to white-label toasters and kettles, electronics can often be repaired at home, for a fraction of the cost of buying new... within reason.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
The long road to repairable tech
Tech repairability isn't a new concept, but it's a rather new debate. Or, at least, it's one that's only recently been at the forefront of the news cycle, under the somewhat beige name 'right to repair'.
For two years now, repairability has been of growing importance to politicians as well as makers. In July 2024, the EU entered into force its 'Directive on repair of goods', and since Europe is a major market for tech companies, changes made for the region have been reflected in tech sold globally.
Designed to go hand-in-hand with several other EU policies on eco-friendly design, the repair directive is designed to make your gadgets easier to fix.
For example, electronics makers are now obliged to repair faulty kit, or make spare parts accessible for a reasonable price, so that third parties can do the repairs for you.
There are several knock-on effects to this and follow-up motions, the most reported being that phone makers will have to fit readily-removable batteries, and manufacturers will have to provide tools so you can make repairs yourself. These rules are changing how companies make their products.
However, there are several exceptions: gadgets designed for wet use, including wearables and headphones won't need to change. And, more importantly, any gadget sold before the European Union's legislation went into effect will of course miss out on these repairability boons.
Some companies may look for loopholes — but not Fairphone
Before repairability was codified in legislation, it was still a focus for certain brands. One of those was Fairphone, a Dutch brand which began life as a campaign about conflict minerals in tech, and now makes phones and headphones. Miquel Ballester, its Head of Product, explained to us why it made the jump into physical devices:
"You can put the most ethically sourced materials in the world into a device, but if it dies in a year and a half because a battery's glued in, you've undone most of the good you just did".
He continued: "In the case of smartphones, earbuds, and headphones, repairability was what made the rest of the mission focus on bringing action into the industry. We've been fighting this fight for over a decade, long before 'right to repair' was something people brought up at dinner."
Fairphone devices are modular, meaning you can easily remove and replace the screen, camera, batteries, or other parts, all without having to extricate them from a tightly-packed device. The brand sells replacement parts online, so you can repair faulty components at home.
According to Ballester, Fairphone found that making its phones repairable didn't mean it had to change the performance and style of its products, but there was an impact on the price: "Designing for modularity means you're working with connectors, seams, and screws instead of glue and epoxy, and that adds a bit of cost compared to a phone that's built to be sealed shut forever".
Don't chase a high IP-rating (when you probably don't need it)
I also asked Ballester if any components or specs struggle in repairable gadgets. "Waterproofing is the one I'd point to first," he explained, railing against the trend of tech companies chasing an IP68 rating.
"Realistically, unless you're taking your phone free diving, IP55 gets you everything you actually need. It holds up against rain, spilled coffee, sweat at the gym, all the situations people actually put their phones through."
So, not IP68, which guarantees you protection for 30 minutes in a meter of water? "Chasing that rating basically forces you into permanent seals and factory-glued seams, because that's still the easiest way to guarantee a device survives being submerged.
"We'd rather give you a device that can be opened and repaired for the next seven years than one that survives a swimming pool once and then can't have its battery replaced. It's a genuinely difficult engineering line to walk, and I won't pretend IP68 wouldn't look nice on a spec sheet, but chasing it would mean compromising the thing we actually care about."
As mentioned, the EU's right to repair changes mean that companies may have to sell tools to repair their gadgets. But for Fairphone, that isn't a problem; they've been designed not to require proprietary tools. A Phillips screwdriver is all you need.
But how repairable is tech really?
Just because a company doesn't make gadget repairability a selling point, doesn't mean that you can't easily fix it. To learn more about the repair process, I visited a local community repair shop called Fixing Factory, which operates several locations in London, UK.
Fixing Factory lets residents bring in broken items to get them repaired, but it also operates as a way to train volunteers in fixing household items.
When I visited the Fixing Factory's Camden location, the streets around the shop were abuzz — England was just hours away from its ultimately-unsuccessful World Cup match against Argentina. But inside the repair shop, a different kind of squad was assembled: a troop of junior repairers (volunteers learning how to repair tech) were being briefed on safety procedures.
As I waited, I got to admire the huge collection of gadgets in various stages of repair (or lack thereof, in the cases of some training toasters). Laptops, vacuum cleaners, radios, even some throwback iPod nanos. Waiting alongside me was an older lady, who'd somehow managed to transport several startlingly-sized antique lamps in a series of backpacks and strollers, all ready to be repaired by the volunteers.
Not all of the Fixing Factory attendees were in training, and I was lucky enough to speak to several of the expert volunteers. They explained to me how to tell if a gadget can be repaired, what to do if you want to fix your tech, and when you should rely on an expert to bring your tech up to spec.
Identifying gadgets as repairable
One repair volunteer, describing themselves as a 'generalist' who liked to fix everything, told me how they'd helped create the teaching material for the trainees in the next room and explained how they work out if a gadget can be fixed in the first place.
"The first thing we do is we will safety check the device. If we've got a plug, we'll make sure we do PAT testing [a standardized way of checking the safety of portable appliances], and then everything goes into an RCD [Residual Current Device, which can instantly turn off power if something goes wrong] before we plug it in, and then we'll do a functional test.
"From there, we'll then diagnose what's going wrong and sit down with a member of the public, and work with them and go: 'okay, tell me the story, what happened, what's not working.'"
From what I was told, about half of the people with broken tech know why it's broken, either because of their own research or because the fault is obvious. And the other half "just have no clue".
The volunteer told me about a recent trial the group conducted, in which they went to a local recycling facility for several months, to log the kind of items thrown away and how much was actually repairable.
"We had far in excess of 70% repairability on e-waste. And so I like to think that's probably reflective of what comes into Fixing Factory locations."
I was staggered by that number; by the sounds of it, well over half of the gadgets we throw away could actually be fixed!
Stats from a similar study carried out by The Restart Project also found that only 12.4% of electrical devices thrown away were truly at the end of their life span. A further 7.2% needed repairs that were deemed too costly to be worthwhile; 9.5% were economical to repair; 36.2% were working just fine, and for the remaining 34.7% it wasn't possible to determine what state of life they were in.
Looking back at that 7,000,000 headphone figure I mentioned before, that'd suggest about 2.5 million of them could get back to a state of working just fine. Truly, the trash is not the first destination for faulty gadgets.
Do (or don't) try this at home
Repair shops such as Fixing Factory are one option for handling your broken tech, but how easy are they to fix at home? (Unless you have a Fairphone product, of course). I spoke to another Fixing Factory volunteer to find out.
Kevin, a student at a local university, told me: "You can literally fix anything if you watch enough YouTube... but it's pretty complicated".
He was one of many volunteers who flagged YouTube and the iFixit channel (and website) specifically, as an invaluable source of information for prospective home repairers. The site publishes teardowns, repair guides, and has an active forum to help you understand just how feasible a home repair is.
Sometimes, even this isn't necessary: "A lot of things are just dirty and need to be cleaned deeply."
This is something I understand all too well; a deep-clean of my home-built PC recently made me realize that I didn't need to buy new parts. It was just dusty.
Kevin gave some sage advice: "Take good notes or good photos to make sure you put [the gadget] back together correctly".
Another volunteer pointed out, though, that online guides and a little clean both play second fiddle to another, more important type of learning: "Sitting down with someone and sharing the experience, I think is something that's very valuable."
Not all tech is worth repairing
Most of the advice so far has pertained to smaller electricals and 'safer' items, but often you want to fix something more complicated. When I asked one volunteer whether home tech repairs were feasible, I was told: "Is it feasible? Yes. Is it safe? Questionable."
There are several dangers involved with lithium-ion batteries, the kind of which you find in most portable gadgets, and their predilection for catching fire is chief amongst them. You don't even have to be repairing them for disaster to strike.
The North London Waste Authority has identified several types of lithium-ion battery-toting gadgets — including smartphones and electric toothbrushes — as major fire risks. According to the organization, which handles waste disposal for seven London boroughs, "electrical items can easily catch fire if they are thrown into general waste and become damaged in waste vehicles".
A spokesperson told me that, across 2025, they saw at least 20 fires which could be linked to battery combustion. They even shared a video of one such incident, which you can see above. Stats from the National Fire Chiefs Council point to there being over 1,200 battery fires across the UK in bin lorries and waste sites that same year.
And it's even worse if you're intentionally trying to fiddle around with them.
"One false move and you can suddenly have a nasty fire," one volunteer told me, adding, "Equally, when you're dealing with mains voltage, you can suffer some serious burns, let alone cardiac arrest. I would encourage anybody to find a friendly electrician, or someone with some qualifications, or a place like Fixing Factory."
Unrepairable tech isn't a manufacturing accident, as the Senior Workshop Manager and Operational Specialist of the Fixing Factory location I visited, Petra Backovska, explained to me. "Sometimes, you find that tech isn't built to be repaired, or repaired easily. And if there's something that wasn't made to be repaired, they make it really hard for you to do it — you can actually break it very, very easily".
Backovska identified cheap electronics manufacturers as a prime culprit for unrepairable tech, where important considerations are forgotten in favor of low costs and mass production. But more complex electronics were just as bad: "There could be things that need to have a CE mark on every item [as opposed to one for the entire gadget]".
This is a mark affixed to most tech products sold in the European Economic Area to show that they're compliant with European health, safety and environmental standards. It'll be familiar to anyone who lives in the area; inspect any gadget within arm's reach, you'll likely find the mark hidden somewhere.
"So if the item doesn't have a CE mark, it's not safe, and we're not going to touch it anyways. So that could increase the number of things that we turn down, because we just don't know if it was manufactured safely."
I was also told that such a mark doesn't necessarily mean tech is safe: "Sometimes the mark is actually fake, and someone just slapped it on and didn't actually do all of the standardized testing in the process, which allowed them to produce something in large quantities very quickly, to sell it very cheap. But that also means that the item is not safe."
So how do you know if something should be repaired at home, or by an expert? Every volunteer advised that, if in doubt, consult an expert or take it to a repair shop: "It's that classic thing: asking is always the safest way."
There's a hard way to learn, and an easy way
Given the risks mentioned, I asked whether repairing tech from home could actually be dangerous, but was told by Backovska, "It doesn't have to be, but you need to have some training and follow the safety steps."
"If you jump into something just guessing things, then you're learning the hard way — and the hard way might be that you give yourself an electric shock. If you don't have experience with repairing, bring it to your local repair group."
I was told that Fixing Factory works with regulators, safety experts and product designers in order to create health and safety processes. These are taught to trainee volunteers, many of whom pass them onto customers whose goods are broken.
One of the volunteers I spoke to helped develop the training courses I got to witness, and told me that gadget-specific skills were often passed along, between volunteers and gadget owners.
The money and the waste
At the heart of the matter, two key reasons define why tech repairs are important. The first is economical: it will often be much cheaper to fix a device than to buy a new one. Second is the environmental impact: e-waste is a massive (and growing) problem, and keeping a hold of old gadgets (by repairing them) reduces the amount of clutter in landfill.
I love to quote a United Nations stat looking at e-waste from 2022: apparently, it'd fill roughly "enough trucks to form a bumper-to-bumper line encircling the equator". Our planet has a gastric band of junk, and hopefully, it'll push us to stop throwing away electronics. It's one of the core drives behind the aforementioned EU legislation.
The Restart Project is a UK-based charity which focuses on the right to repair electronics; it lobbies for legislation, helps organize repair groups (like the Fixing Factory I visited) and educates on the state of electronics. I spoke to Fiona Dear, co-Director at The Restart Project, to learn where repairable tech is going in the future.
"We have seen a bit of change [from companies] in recent years, and that's generally as a response to legislation. Even if the legislation isn't enacted, [manufacturers' changes are] in anticipation of legislation."
At the moment though (and in Europe, at least), this is limited: "There's only really legislation for two kinds of products. The first is white goods like dishwashers, and there's been legislation in place for a few years now. And it's just expanded to smartphones and tablets in Europe — that's why we're seeing a difference.
"Unfortunately, there's nothing much on the horizon for other product categories". That's why it's such a shame that, as mentioned earlier, wireless earbuds have seen a repairability exemption.
A problem of parts pairing
When I asked how technological changes are affecting repairability, one massive problem reared its head, which Dear called out specifically: "Parts pairing".
Parts pairing is a software limitation some brands apply to their devices. The gadgets will recognize when non-native parts are added, and throw up an error message when you try to use them.
For example, a phone might not let you use a new screen, a pair of headphones might reject their drivers, or a laptop might not play with a battery you install. In fact, software seems to be public enemy number one for tech repairability at the moment.
"A dishwasher or even a toaster, might have some kind of smart element in it," Dear explained, "which means it's dependent on software, and software isn't designed to last for as long as the mechanics of the product".
As iFixit points out in its guide to parts pairing, this is done by brands to encourage you to use its own repair services, instead of third-party ones (or repairing your own tech at home, using replacement parts). Often, the brand in question has unique access to make these error messages disappear. Dear flagged refurbished smartphones as being especially susceptible to this practice.
"Parts pairing is, in my personal opinion, one of the more cynical practices in this industry", Fairphone's Miquel Ballester explained. "Every component we ship, whether it's a battery in a Fairphone or bud and case battery in Fairbuds, is built to be freely interchangeable".
But software limitations remain an issue for tech longevity. "The repair experts who point out that software is the real bottleneck are right. It's exactly why we also treat long-term software support as inseparable from the repairability story".
The brand's latest mobile, the Fairphone 6, has a guaranteed 8 major Android updates, one of the longest life spans pledged by an Android maker. For many years, any more than two years' updates were a rarity, but nowadays companies are offering more and more updates. The Samsung Galaxy S26 and Google Pixel 10 series, for example, both have 7 years in the can.
Become a TechRadar Insider by simply clicking 'Join Now' at the top of this page. Have a question? Please email membership@techradar.com
It takes a change of attitude
When I told peers that I was working on a tech repair piece, I received some intriguing reactions. Some view it as a great way to keep your gadgets ticking along (as it should be), but stories of cowboy repairers abound.
Recently, we covered a story about a Best Buy repairer who downloaded private photos from a broken iPhone, and some people I spoke to seemed to harbor suspicion towards the rows of mobile phone repair shops which line some British high streets.
But the high proliferation of gadget repair stores is indicative of something different: a strong demand for our gadgets to keep working longer. Tech shops aren't fronts for dodgy dealings; they fix the devices we use every day, which is probably a more lucrative market than narcotics or single-use vapes.
Over the last few years, the rise of AI has driven up memory prices, causing gadgets to cost a lot more money, and new purchases to be more and more of a treat. You've surely noticed that electronics purchases nowadays cost a lot more (and bundle in some useless AI tools as a consolation prize, but that's a gripe for another day).
With no sign of that slowing down, gadget repairs are only going to be more and more important. And so a change is needed: a change in attitude to tech fixing, a change in our own skill sets so we're able to do so at home, and a change in legislation so that companies have to make it easier for us to mend our ailing electronics.

articles.title: 5 películas de terror que seguro no conoces y que puedes ver ahora mismo en streaming
articles.text:
El género de terror atraviesa una de sus épocas más lucrativas y creativas. Lo que le ha convertido en un pilar fundamental del cine en la actualidad. Con experimentos como Weapons, dirigida por Zach Cregger, y Los pecadores de Ryan Coogler, las historias espeluznantes han logrado una nueva importancia. Eso, mientras éxitos de sagas queridas como Expediente Warren: El último rito dejaban claro que el terror era algo más que solo accidentes afortunados. Sin olvidar cine independiente del género como Devuélvemela y Obsesión.
Esta combinación demuestra que el horror actual no solo confía en la nostalgia de sagas recurrentes como Scream o Insidious. A la vez, se sostiene sobre la frescura de nuevos realizadores que conectan con los miedos de las audiencias modernas. Pero sobre todo, que el cine de terror contemporáneo es mucho más que solo historias creadas para provocar sobresaltos y aterrorizar por medios sencillos. Lo que hace de los más curiosos estrenos, una combinación entre temática, apartado visual y una elegante visión de lo terrorífico.
Todo un festín para fanáticos que además, deja a su paso una buena cantidad de cintas ideales para satisfacer incluso el gusto cinematográfico más raro. Si ese es tu caso, esta lista es para ti. Te dejamos cinco películas raras de terror que seguramente no conoces y que puedes ver ahora mismo en streaming. De una pieza de arte visual a lo más novedoso del horror folk. Todo para los fanáticos de terror de hueso rojo que disfrutan de un tipo de cinta sorprendente y que los servicios por suscripción hacen mucho más accesible.
Gaua (Prime Video)
Este recorrido mitológico por el País Vasco del siglo XVII es una de las grandes películas de terror que puedes encontrar en streaming. Escrita y dirigida por el aclamado cineasta Paul Urkijo Alijo, la producción sigue los pasos de Kattalin (Yune Nogueiras). Esta, una joven que huye de su violento esposo y que termina perdida en la densa penumbra del bosque. Para después, enfrentar a lo sobrenatural desde una óptica por completo nueva.
El gran triunfo de Urkijo radica en su capacidad para dignificar y empoderar la figura de las brujas. Además, de introducir de manera orgánica a seres espectrales del folclore como Gaueko o Inguma. Para lo que huye de los clichés inquisitoriales tradicionales. Visualmente apabullante, la cinta destaca por una impecable fotografía a cargo de Gorka Gómez Andreu. También, un soberbio uso de efectos especiales prácticos, maquillaje y vestuario, apartados que le valieron múltiples nominaciones en los prestigiosos Premios Goya.
Primate (Movistar+)
Esta rareza del subgénero del terror de supervivencia animal, sorprende por su premisa compacta, salvaje y sumamente eficaz. Dirigida por el cineasta británico Johannes Roberts, la cinta destaca por su ritmo implacable. También por un guion que emula de forma directa la tensión claustrofóbica de clásicos literarios y cinematográficos como Cujo de Stephen King.
La trama se sitúa en un idílico entorno tropical en Hawái, donde Lucy (Johnny Sequoyah) planea disfrutar de unas tranquilas vacaciones. Sin embargo, la atmósfera festiva se torna en una pesadilla sangrienta cuando Ben, el inteligente chimpancé mascota de la familia, es mordido por una mangosta rabiosa. Lo que desata un brote de agresión salvaje e incontrolable.
Primate evita la solemnidad pretenciosa, apostando por un festival de tensión pura y cruda. Roberts saca el máximo provecho de un elenco sólido que incluye a Jessica Alexander y al ganador del Óscar Troy Kotsur. Este, interpretado de manera entrañable, al padre sordo de la protagonista. Si estás buscando una rareza del género, esta es ideal para ti.
Keeper (Movistar+)
Dirigida por Osgood Perkins (reconocido por éxitos como Longlegs y The Monkey), es una de esas películas de terror que pasan desapercibidas. Pero que terminan por convertirse en pequeños clásicos. Con un ajustado presupuesto de 6 millones de dólares, la cinta brilla al transformar una premisa aparentemente sencilla en una experiencia surrealista y profundamente asfixiante. La trama sigue a Liz (Tatiana Maslany) y Malcolm (Rossif Sutherland), una pareja que decide celebrar su aniversario con una escapada de fin de semana. Lo que les lleva a una cabaña completamente aislada en el bosque.
Sin embargo, la aparente tranquilidad se quiebra por completo cuando Malcolm debe regresar repentinamente a la ciudad por una emergencia. Por lo que deja a Liz sola en la propiedad ante la manifestación de presencias siniestras y un mal indescriptible que devela los oscuros e históricos secretos del lugar. Ideal para fanáticos del gran plot-twist final.
Stopmotion (Prime Video)
Escrita y dirigida por el aclamado cortometrajista británico Robert Morgan, la cinta explora las fronteras entre la cordura, el arte macabro y la cruda realidad. La trama sigue los pasos de Ella Blake (Aisling Franciosi), una talentosa animadora atrapada bajo la absorbente sombra de su dominante madre. Esta, una leyenda de la animación.
Tras una tragedia familiar, Ella se vuelca obsesivamente en la creación de un retorcido cortometraje con marionetas hechas de materiales grotescos. Un proyecto que poco a poco empieza a cobrar una siniestra vida propia. La gran genialidad de la producción radica en utilizar la extenuante y milimétrica técnica del cuadro por cuadro (stop-motion) no solo como un formato visual. También, como una retorcida alegoría sobre el trauma heredado, el aislamiento absoluto y el perfeccionismo destructivo.
Morgan combina de forma magistral secuencias de acción real con una animación espeluznante y de texturas orgánicas. Además, con un sobresaliente diseño de sonido que acentúa cada crujido y deformación acústica. El filme prescinde por completo de los sustos fáciles para edificar una atmósfera de pesadilla pura y existencial. Es una auténtica obra cumbre sobre la locura del creador que atrapa y fascina de principio a fin.
El ritual (Netflix)
Dirigida por David Bruckner y escrita por Joe Barton esta adaptación de la aclamada novela homónima de Adam Neville, es ideal para los amantes del folk horror. En especial, por la capacidad de la cinta de entrelazar de forma orgánica el terror sobrenatural con un desgarrador drama sobre la culpa, el duelo y la cobardía. La trama sigue a cuatro amigos de la universidad que se reúnen para hacer senderismo en los densos y desolados bosques de Suecia. Todo como homenaje a un amigo trágicamente asesinado.
Sin embargo, tras tomar un atajo equivocado, el grupo queda atrapado en un laberinto natural. En medio de la cual, una presencia ancestral y malévola comienza a acecharlos y a desenterrar sus peores traumas nocturnos. Pero en lugar de ser evidente, la obra prefiere edificar una atmósfera de tensión asfixiante e incómoda basada en símbolos de ocultismo pagano. Sin embargo, su gran éxito es la criatura final, Moder: un gigante jötunn de la mitología nórdica. Una entidad retorcida de impresionante diseño visual que se alza como uno de los más creativos del cine de horror moderno.

articles.title: TechCrunch Mobility: Two roads diverged — for robotaxis | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Welcome back to TechCrunch Mobility, your hub for the future of transportation and now, more than ever, the role AI is playing in it. To get this in your inbox, sign up here for free — just click TechCrunch Mobility!
TechCrunch covered a couple of stories this week that illustrate the countervailing forces at play within the autonomous vehicle industry. The federal government is hitting the accelerator while state and local officials are pumping the brakes on autonomous vehicles.
The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration made a series of autonomous vehicle technology announcements designed to cut red tape and accelerate the development and deployment of this technology (my article describes many of its actions). The one that got the most attention was the agency’s decision to give Zoox a temporary exemption from eight federal motor vehicle safety standards, which will finally allow the company to charge customers for rides in its custom-built robotaxi.
The importance of this can’t be understated. This was one of the last remaining regulatory hurdles Zoox needed to clear before launching a commercial robotaxi service. And according to the company, paid rides are imminent. The company will start charging for rides in Las Vegas first.
Meanwhile, Waymo and other robotaxi operators are facing increased scrutiny over how their autonomous vehicles interact with emergency responders, a regulatory risk that’s becoming harder for the industry to shrug off. As I have noted before, San Francisco mayor Daniel Lurie asked state regulators to bolster rules for autonomous vehicles nearly two weeks after Waymo robotaxis became immobile in heavy July 4 traffic, ran out of power, and blocked key streets, further compounding the gridlock.
This week, Rep. Kevin Mullin (D-Calif.) proposed a bill that would direct federal regulators to establish minimum national safety standards for autonomous vehicle operators.
“We have seen disturbing, and frankly, an unacceptable number of incidents where autonomous vehicles inadvertently interfere with emergency responders,” Mullin said during the press conference, which Lurie also spoke at.
So here we are, a push forward, and nope, a pull back. And in the middle is the AV industry.
What do you think? Send me an email with your view at kirsten.korosec@techcrunch.com.
Deals!
Lucid has landed more Saudi money, this time from Prince Al Waleed bin Talal Al Saud, a member of the Saudi royal family. The billionaire prince purchased a little more than 19 million shares, or about 5%, of Lucid Motors, according to a regulatory filing.
Elon Musk’s tunneling startup The Boring Company is in talks to raise a $4 billion funding round at a valuation of $20 billion.
Terminal, a Toronto-based startup that provides telematics data infrastructure for the commercial fleet industry, raised $20 million in a Series A round led by Battery Ventures. New strategic investors Intact Private Capital and Penske, as well as returning backers Y Combinator and Wayfinder Ventures, also participated.
Notable reads and other tidbits
Alaska Airlines CEO and president Ben Minicucci joined Lyft’s board of directors.
The nascent on-demand drone-delivery industry had a busy week. Walmart and Alphabet’s Wing drone delivery started service across Central Florida, and Flytrex announced a partnership with autonomic logistics platform Nash. But the biggest announcement was about DoorDash, which said it was building a drone delivery business, including its own aircraft, as part of an effort developed by its robotics and autonomy team. This will eventually operate within the company’s delivery app.
Ferrari might have received a lot of hate for its first all-electric vehicle, the Luce, but the criticism didn’t dampen sales. Ferrari hit this year’s sales target for the Luce in just two months.
Florida was awarded $200 million under the federal National Electric Vehicle Infrastructure program, but the money never made it to charging infrastructure for electric cars. Instead, the state is using the money to build 32 landing pads with charging stations for electric vertical take-off and landing aircraft, or eVTOLs.
London is shaping up to be the next robotaxi battleground. Baidu has started testing autonomous vehicles in London as part of its partnership with Lyft and Freenow, the taxi and multi-mobility app that the ride-hailing company now owns. The companies plan to invite the public to hail their robotaxis in 2027. Meanwhile, others are also preparing to launch. In April, Waymo began testing its autonomous vehicles with human safety operators in the city. Uber and its self-driving tech partner, Wayve, also announced plans to launch a robotaxi service in London this year.
Rivian spinoff Also will finally start delivering its first e-bikes to customers next week, after months of delays related to unspecified supply chain issues.
In yet another hint that a Tesla-SpaceX merger is imminent, the EV maker is considering selling off its China business ahead of a SpaceX merger, according to the Wall Street Journal. Meanwhile, Tesla hit a new milestone and built its 10 millionth EV.
Waymo robotaxis started to return to freeways, more than two months after the company stopped driving these high-speed roads over concerns about how its autonomous vehicles behaved near construction zones.
One more thing …
There was a time when this newsletter was chock-full of electric vehicle news, much of it centered on ambitious plans from U.S. automakers GM and Ford. Both companies ramped up spending and formed joint ventures to build battery and EV factories, in an effort to shift their portfolios to ones filled with electric cars, trucks, and SUVs. But as those plans have retreated, so has the talk.
TechCrunch teamed up with Hudson Labs, a New York-based financial research firm, to analyze the last seven years of GM and Ford quarterly earnings calls and found that both companies are talking about EVs at a lower rate than they did before the pandemic.
The upshot: While GM and Ford still sell EVs and have new models in their product pipelines, their collective focus has shifted, and it shows in the data. Check out the story, which includes two interactive graphs.

articles.title: Rachika Nayar’s Heaven Come Crashing is an instrumental epic of desperate longing
articles.text:
Two minutes and thirty seconds into the title track of Rachika Nayar’s Heaven Come Crashing, an absolutely massive drum and bass beat drops. As a fan of Nayar’s debut record Our Hands Against The Dusk, it caught me off guard. That album has no percussion on it at all. Heaven Come Crashing is almost entirely drum-free, too. There are some rapid-fire mechanical hi-hats on the second track, “Tetramorph,” and the back half of track six, “Gayatri,” has what sounds like a snare buried deep in the mix. But it isn’t until track seven that Nayar delivers an unexpected drum explosion, before immediately retreating to the soothing wash of “Sleepless,” just one song later.
Rachika Nayar’s Heaven Come Crashing is an instrumental epic of desperate longing
It’s disgusted with its own reckless romanticism.
It’s disgusted with its own reckless romanticism.
Nayar’s unique brand of guitar-heavy ambient-adjacent music plays almost like a version of M83 from an alternate universe. One where instead of turning to ’80s pop music for inspiration, Anthony Gonzalez mined his instrumental epics for every last drop of emotion. Heaven Come Crashing is as emotionally heavy as the title would imply but uses surprisingly few words to get there. The only vocals come courtesy of Maria BC, who floats over the title track and the stunning album closer “Our Wretched Fate,” where she worldlessly belts out her laments.
There are lyrics on “Heaven Come Crashing,” but they’re almost indecipherable as Maria BC whispers beneath an ocean of flailing guitar lines and sparkling drones:
Is it morning?
I don’t remember going to sleep
How can we face the day
Like this?
You throw down your arms and count to see
How deep it is
Instead of words, Nayar turns to heavily processed guitar, lonesome textures, and the occasional burst of trance chords to capture the desperate longing at the album’s core. But the album is also an indictment of the sort of abandon that often accompanies unbridled passion. It’s bookended by “Our Wretched Fantasy” and “Our Wretched Fate,” betraying a certain disgust for its own emotional recklessness. Track three isn’t “Death and Love”; it’s “Death and Limerence” — opting to spotlight unhealthy romantic obsession rather than fulfilling emotional partnership, through U2-esque guitar lines that eventually drown beneath heavily reverbed and out-of-tune tremolo-picked notes.
That’s followed by the unease of “Nausea,” which builds from an unsteady drone to maximalist panic of ’90s synths and one of the simplest and prettiest guitar melodies on the record. The ambient emo of “Promises” follows, leading into “Gayatri,” which ratchets up the energy and serves as a bridge to the explosive title track.
Rachika Nayar’s Heaven Come Crashing is available on Bandcamp and most major streaming services, including Apple Music, Spotify, YouTube Music, Qobuz, and Deezer.

articles.title: Parti en toupie dans l'espace, le remorqueur LINK évite le pire, mais tout n'est pas réglé
articles.text:
Le remorqueur spatial LINK n’est pas encore totalement tiré d’affaire, mais la NASA et Katalyst Space ont enfin pu pousser un ouf de soulagement prudent ces jours-ci. En effet, alors que la mission de sauvetage du télescope spatial Swift était très mal engagée, les équipes au sol sont parvenues à en reprendre partiellement la maîtrise.
Des poussées ciblées pour calmer la toupie
Le problème ? LINK était entré dans une rotation incontrôlée après la perte de deux de ses roues de réaction servant à le stabiliser. Devenu une toupie, l’engin n’était alors plus en mesure d’approcher Swift pour le relancer sur une orbite plus haute. Katalyst, l’entreprise qui a conçu LINK, a alors dû se servir de sa propulsion.
Dans une mise à jour publiée le 31 juillet, l’entreprise américaine indique avoir utilisé un propulseur électrique à effet Hall monté sur un cardan orientable deux axes. La manœuvre a globalement porté ses fruits : en l’espace de 48 heures, une série d’allumages successifs a permis de réduire la vitesse de rotation.
Concrètement, celle-ci est passée de 9 à moins de 4 degrés par seconde. Il reste encore quelques poussées à produire pour stabiliser totalement LINK.
Un pilotage à réinventer et un rendez-vous repoussé
Mais freiner la toupie ne règle toutefois qu’une partie du problème. Privé de ses gyroscopes principaux, le véhicule a un problème d’orientation à long terme. Mais, comme l’indique la NASA, les ingénieurs développent un tout nouveau logiciel de contrôle d’attitude en réaffectant les propulseurs encore opérationnels.
Ce nouveau système de guidage sera testé en simulation au sol avant d’être téléversé directement en orbite.
Toutes ces péripéties à des centaines de kilomètres d’altitude entraînent une forte modification du calendrier du rendez-vous spatial avec Swift. Prévue début août au départ, la tentative d’approche est repoussée vers la fin du mois. En clair, le sauvetage de Swift est toujours d’actualité, à condition que LINK arrive à bien s’orienter.

articles.title: Llevamos décadas alargando los días en la Tierra sin darnos cuenta y eso no es algo bueno
articles.text:
Hace tiempo que sabemos que el cambio climático está alargando nuestros días. Cuando los casquetes polares se derriten, hay más agua líquida en los océanos, por lo que el peso total de la misma se redistribuye, complicando y ralentizando el giro de la Tierra sobre su propio eje. Como consecuencia, tenemos días más largos. Es un fenómeno natural, ya que, al fin y al cabo, en las épocas de más calor es normal que el hielo se derrita. Esto, además, se complementa con la influencia gravitatoria de la Luna, que contribuye también a reducir la velocidad de rotación terrestre.
Hasta ahora, el efecto de la Luna era mayor que el del deshielo. No obstante, según un estudio publicado recientemente, las tornas pueden cambiarse pronto. Como resultado, nuestros días están siendo más largos que nunca. A efectos de seguridad no supone nada. No nos va a afectar, pues es una diferencia minimísima. Sin embargo, es un efecto medible que nos demuestra que el cambio climático está llegando demasiado lejos. De hecho, las noches sin dormir que nos está provocando sí que nos hacen sentir que los días son demasiado largos.
1,33 milisegundos por siglo. El estudio que se acaba de publicar ha sido realizado por científicos de la Universidad de Viena y la ETH Zúrich. En él, no solo han calculado la velocidad de rotación terrestre actual, sino que han llevado a cabo modelos computacionales que les han permitido compararla con dicha velocidad a lo largo de la historia. Así, han visto que actualmente los días se están alargando 1,33 milisegundos por siglo. Puede parecer poquísimo y realmente lo es, pero es un dato que significa mucho.
Un patinador con los brazos abiertos. Cuando los polos están congelados, hay una gran cantidad de masa concentrada en ellos. Sin embargo, cuando estos se derriten, parte del agua que los forman se extiende por el océano y llega mucho más lejos. Esto afecta a la rotación terrestre como el baile de un patinador sobre hielo. Cuando estos juntan los brazos al cuerpo, concentran toda su masa sobre el centro y giran más deprisa. En cambio, cuando abren los brazos, giran poco a poco más despacio. Todo esto se debe a un fenómeno de la física conocido como conservación del momento angular.
Hemos visto que la ralentización de la velocidad de rotación no es nueva. Sin embargo, nunca ha ocurrido a las tasas actuales, según lo que han observado estos científicos.
Los fósiles que tenían la clave de los días más largos. Para reconstruir la velocidad de rotación terrestre a lo largo de la historia, estos científicos se fijaron en los fósiles de foraminíferos bentónicos. Estos son organismos microscópicos que viven en el fondo océanico y construyen una concha de carbonato cálcico. En este proceso, incorporan oxígeno procedente del agua del mar, que puede venir en dos formatos: el isótopo O-16 y el O-18. La proporción entre uno y otro depende de factores como la temperatura del agua o la cantidad de la misma que estaba anteriormente en estado sólido, en forma de hielo. Por ejemplo, cuando hay más hielo en los polos el agua es más rica en O-18.
Teniendo todo esto en cuenta, se pueden establecer los niveles de hielo y agua líquida que había en distintos periodos, simplemente estudiando la composición de estas conchas fosilizadas. Después, gracias a modelos informáticos, se puede calcular cuánto duraba el día en todos esos periodos.
Datos sin precedentes. En total, estos científicos han analizado la velocidad de rotación terrestre y los consiguientes cambios de duración del día de los últimos 3,6 millones de años. En ningún momento ha habido un efecto tan marcado como el que se ha medido entre los años 2000 y 2020.
A veces también se acelera. Cabe destacar que los propios procesos internos del planeta, como el flujo de fluidos en el núcleo terrestre, pueden contribuir a que el giro de nuestro planeta se acelere de vez en cuando. La velocidad de rotación terrestre no es tan fija como podríamos llegar a creer. Aun así, hay una tendencia que nos sirve como clara señal de que el cambio climático inducido por los seres humanos está sometiendo al planeta a una presión a la que no se ha sometido nunca. Aunque los días más largos no sean peligrosos, todo lo demás que conlleva esa presión sí lo es. Por eso es esencial actuar contra el cambio climático.

Understanding the Role of IT Consulting in Business Efficiency
In today’s fast-paced digital landscape, businesses must leverage technology effectively to maintain operational efficiency and competitive advantage. IT consulting has emerged as a critical component in this endeavor, offering expert guidance and tailored solutions to streamline everyday operations. By aligning IT strategies with business objectives, organizations can optimize workflows, reduce downtime, and enhance overall productivity.
One effective approach is partnering with specialized firms that provide comprehensive IT advisory services. For example, businesses seeking expert insights can explore enkompas for technology consulting, which offers tailored strategies to meet diverse operational needs. These consultants assess existing infrastructure, identify bottlenecks, and recommend scalable solutions that align with long-term growth plans.
IT consulting goes beyond mere technical support; it involves a holistic approach to integrating technology into every facet of business operations. This includes understanding the unique challenges of each organization, industry-specific compliance requirements, and future trends that could impact the business landscape. By doing so, IT consultants help companies not only solve immediate issues but also build resilient systems that support innovation and agility.
Moreover, the demand for IT consulting continues to grow as digital transformation accelerates. A recent report indicates that the global IT consulting market is projected to reach $605 billion by 2027, growing at a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 8.5%. This growth underscores the increasing reliance on expert IT guidance to navigate complex technological environments.
Key IT Consulting Strategies for Operational Excellence
Implementing robust IT consulting strategies involves several key elements that contribute to smoother daily operations:
- Comprehensive IT Infrastructure Assessment
A thorough evaluation of existing IT systems is foundational. Consultants analyze network architecture, software applications, hardware capabilities, and security protocols. This assessment uncovers inefficiencies and vulnerabilities, enabling the creation of a customized roadmap for improvement.
For instance, an infrastructure assessment might reveal outdated servers causing frequent slowdowns or security gaps that expose sensitive data. Addressing these issues early prevents costly downtime and data breaches, which can severely disrupt business continuity.
- Cloud Integration and Management
Cloud technology adoption continues to accelerate, with 94% of enterprises using cloud services in some capacity as of 2023. Effective IT consulting ensures seamless migration to cloud platforms, optimizing resource allocation and facilitating remote collaboration.
Cloud integration not only reduces the need for on-premises hardware but also offers scalability and flexibility, allowing businesses to adjust resources based on demand. Consultants help select appropriate cloud models-public, private, or hybrid-and manage ongoing operations to maximize uptime and security.
- Cybersecurity Enhancement
With cyberattacks increasing by 38% year-over-year, robust cybersecurity measures are indispensable. IT consultants implement advanced threat detection, employee training, and compliance protocols to safeguard sensitive data and maintain operational continuity.
Cybersecurity strategies often include deploying firewalls, intrusion detection systems, multi-factor authentication, and regular vulnerability assessments. Additionally, consultants foster a security-conscious culture by educating employees about phishing and other social engineering threats, which remain primary attack vectors.
- Automation and Process Optimization
Automating repetitive tasks reduces errors and frees up employee time for strategic initiatives. IT consulting firms help identify automation opportunities using tools like robotic process automation (RPA) and AI-driven analytics, driving efficiency gains across departments.
For example, automating invoice processing or customer service chatbots can accelerate workflows and improve accuracy. Consultants also analyze existing processes to eliminate redundancies and optimize resource allocation, ensuring technology investments deliver maximum value.
- Vendor and Technology Selection
Choosing the right technology partners is crucial. Businesses can benefit from tech consulting with FTI Services, which specializes in guiding companies through technology procurement and integration, ensuring solutions align with organizational goals and budget constraints.
Selecting vendors involves evaluating product capabilities, service-level agreements, support quality, and cost-effectiveness. IT consultants bring industry knowledge and negotiation expertise to secure favorable terms and maintain strong vendor relationships, which are vital for long-term success.
Benefits of Engaging Professional IT Consultants
Partnering with experienced IT consultants yields multiple benefits that directly impact daily operations:
– Improved System Reliability: Proactive monitoring and maintenance minimize downtime, ensuring consistent access to critical systems.
– Cost Savings: Strategic IT planning reduces unnecessary expenditures and maximizes return on technology investments.
– Scalability: Consultants design flexible infrastructures that scale with business growth, avoiding costly future overhauls.
– Enhanced Employee Productivity: Streamlined workflows and user-friendly technologies empower staff to perform at their best.
– Regulatory Compliance: Expertise in industry standards helps organizations avoid penalties and reputational damage.
According to a recent study, businesses that utilize IT consulting services report a 50% faster resolution of technical issues and a 30% increase in operational efficiency. These improvements translate into measurable competitive advantages, including faster time-to-market and higher customer satisfaction.
In addition, IT consultants often bring fresh perspectives that challenge entrenched practices and encourage innovation. Their external viewpoint helps identify opportunities for digital transformation that internal teams might overlook due to familiarity bias. This can lead to the adoption of cutting-edge technologies such as machine learning, Internet of Things (IoT), or blockchain to further enhance operations.
Implementing IT Consulting Recommendations Effectively
To maximize the value of IT consulting, organizations should focus on structured implementation and continuous improvement. This includes:
– Clear Communication: Establishing transparent channels between consultants, IT teams, and management to ensure alignment.
– Defined KPIs: Setting measurable goals to track progress and demonstrate the impact of new initiatives.
– Change Management: Preparing employees for transitions through training and support to facilitate adoption.
– Regular Reviews: Scheduling periodic assessments to adjust strategies based on evolving business needs and technological advancements.
Successful implementation also hinges on executive sponsorship and cross-departmental collaboration. When leadership actively supports IT initiatives and encourages cooperation between IT and business units, projects are more likely to succeed and deliver lasting benefits.
Moreover, organizations should cultivate a culture of agility and continuous learning to keep pace with rapid technological change. This means investing in ongoing staff training and staying informed about emerging trends and best practices in IT management. For example, encouraging certifications in cloud technologies or cybersecurity among IT staff can keep the organization prepared for future challenges.
Conclusion
IT consulting is a vital catalyst for smoother everyday operations, enabling businesses to harness technology strategically and efficiently. By leveraging expert advice from providers such as and, organizations can optimize their IT environments, safeguard assets, and enhance productivity. In an era where technology underpins every aspect of business, embracing proven IT consulting strategies is essential for sustained success and operational excellence.
As digital transformation continues to reshape industries, companies that proactively engage IT consultants position themselves to adapt quickly, innovate continuously, and outperform competitors. Whether it’s through cloud adoption, cybersecurity fortification, or process automation, the right consulting partnership can turn technological challenges into opportunities for growth and efficiency.

articles.title: Un débris spatial retombe chaque jour sur Terre, et la menace grossit
articles.text:
L’orbite basse fonctionne depuis 1957 comme un grenier dont personne ne vide jamais les cartons. Satellites hors service, étages de fusée, boulons, éclats de peinture : tout ce qui monte y séjourne des années, parfois des décennies, avant de redescendre. On y recense au bas mot 36 500 objets de plus de dix centimètres, environ un million entre un et dix centimètres, et quelque 130 millions de fragments millimétriques. Le grenier déborde, et il se vide par le bas.
Lire aussi : Pourquoi Starlink va faire descendre plus de 4 000 satellites un peu plus près de la Terre
Chaque jour, un morceau du ciel redescend
Sur les cinquante dernières années, la moyenne tourne autour d’un débris catalogué retombant quotidiennement vers la Terre. Rien que pour 2024, le compteur européen a enregistré la rentrée atmosphérique de 1 200 objets intacts et de plusieurs millions de fragments. L’écrasante majorité finit en poussière incandescente à cinquante kilomètres d’altitude, et les océans couvrent commodément 71 % de la surface du globe (la statistique rassure moins quand on habite les 29 % restants).
Les exceptions se sont multipliées à un rythme… inconfortable. En mars 2024, une batterie larguée depuis la Station spatiale internationale a traversé le toit d’une maison de Naples, en Floride. En décembre de la même année, un anneau métallique de 500 kilos et deux mètres et demi de diamètre s’est posé au Kenya. En février 2025, des morceaux d’un étage de Falcon 9 ont survolé l’Angleterre et la Scandinavie avant de s’écraser en Pologne. Trois mois plus tard, la sonde soviétique Kosmos 482 rentrait dans l’atmosphère après cinquante-trois ans d’orbite, faute d’avoir jamais atteint Vénus. Et en juillet, des sphères métalliques repêchées sur le littoral australien ont été attribuées à un corps de fusée étranger, sans que personne sache dire lequel avec certitude.
Lire aussi : Panne en orbite : le satellite censé sauver un télescope de la NASA est en danger
Ces objets survivent mieux qu’avant, et ce n’est pas un hasard. Les matériaux qui font les bons vaisseaux (fibre de carbone, titane, réservoirs composites sous pression) sont précisément ceux qui résistent à la chaleur. Plus l’industrie spatiale progresse, plus ses déchets arrivent entiers.
Et si le vrai danger, c’était pour les avions ?
Le décompte le plus inquiétant ne concerne pas le sol puisque mi-2024, plus de 2 300 corps de fusée tournaient encore en orbite, tous promis à une rentrée un jour ou l’autre à une date que personne ne maîtrise vraiment. Des chercheurs ont calculé la probabilité qu’un de ces débris percute un avion de ligne : elle reste faible, mais les conséquences d’un tel impact rendent l’exercice moins théorique qu’il n’y paraît.
Un appareil en croisière traverse le ciel à 900 km/h, ce qui suffit à transformer une particule anodine en projectile, un peu comme un avion pris dans un nuage de cendres volcaniques. Les gros débris ne sont donc pas les seuls dont il faut se soucier Les autorités aériennes se retrouvent devant un arbitrage désagréable : fermer un couloir aérien par précaution coûte cher et désorganise tout un réseau, ne rien fermer revient à parier. En novembre 2022, la rentrée incontrôlée d’un lanceur chinois avait déjà bousculé le trafic, sans qu’aucune règle internationale ne dise vraiment qui décide quoi.
Vos chances personnelles de recevoir un morceau de fusée sur la tête restent infimes, et le resteront. Celles de voir un jour votre vol dérouté pour cause de ferraille orbitale, en revanche, progressent à chaque lancement.

articles.title: Stop graphing everything: When GraphRAG actually beats vector RAG
articles.text: If you have built anything with retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) in the last two years, you have lived its central frustration: You chop your documents into chunks, embed them, retrieve the top few that look similar to the question, and hand them to the model. For “What was our Q3 refund policy?” This works beautifully. For “What are the recurring themes across two years of customer complaints?” it falls flat — because no single chunk contains the answer. The fashionable fix is GraphRAG : Instead of feeding the model isolated snippets, you first build a knowledge graph of the entities and relationships in your corpus, then use that structure as context. The pitch is seductive. But seductive pitches deserve scrutiny, so I went through the evidence — the original Microsoft paper plus four independent benchmark studies — to answer a simple question: When you swap text chunks for a context graph, do answers actually get better? The short version: Yes, substantially — but only for the right kind of question, and not for free. Let me show you the receipts. Why text chunks hit a wall Standard vector RAG retrieves the k passages most similar to your query. That design has three structural blind spots: It can’t connect the dots. When an answer requires joining facts that live in different passages through a shared entity, chunks embedded in isolation never reveal the link. It’s blind to global questions. “What are the main themes?” needs the whole corpus, but similarity search only returns the handful of chunks that superficially resemble the question. It severs context at chunk boundaries. The relationships and hierarchy that complex reasoning depends on are exactly what chunking throws away. Microsoft Research framed this crisply when they introduced GraphRAG: Baseline RAG “struggles to connect the dots” and performs poorly when asked to “holistically understand summarized semantic concepts over large data collections.” What a context graph changes GraphRAG attacks the problem before any question is asked. During indexing, a large language model (LLM) reads every chunk and extracts entities, relationships, and claims, assembling them into a weighted knowledge graph. It then runs community detection (the Leiden algorithm ) to cluster the graph into a hierarchy of related topics, and pre-writes a natural-language summary for each community. At query time, those summaries do the heavy lifting. Each relevant community drafts a partial answer (the “map” step), the partials are ranked and merged (the “reduce” step), and the model synthesizes a final response grounded in structure rather than in a few cherry-picked snippets. Variants like HippoRAG take a different route, using the graph plus a Personalized PageRank walk to find the right passages — but the core idea is the same: Let relationships, not just cosine similarity, decide what context the model sees. The evidence: Four studies, one pattern 1. Global sense making: The headline win Microsoft pitted GraphRAG head-to-head against naïve RAG on global, “make sense of the whole corpus” questions over million-token datasets, with an LLM acting as judge across three axes: Comprehensiveness, diversity, and empowerment. GraphRAG won 72 to 83% of comprehensiveness comparisons and 62 to 82% of diversity comparisons against vector RAG . Its highest-level summaries used up to 97% fewer tokens than processing the source text directly. That is not a rounding-error improvement. On exactly the kind of question that breaks text-chunk RAG, the graph wins two out of three times or better. 2. Multi-hop retrieval: The graph finds what chunks miss The second piece of evidence is about retrieval quality: Does the right supporting passage even make it into the top results? On the standard multi-hop QA benchmarks (MuSiQue, HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA), graph-guided retrieval lifts Recall@5 dramatically: Average Recall@5 climbs from 73.4% (naïve RAG) to 87.8% (graph-guided), a +19.6 point gain. The biggest jumps come on the hardest, cross-document sets: +31 points on MuSiQue and +28 points on 2Wiki . HippoRAG reports up to a 20% accuracy improvement on multi-hop QA, at 10–20× lower cost and 6–13× faster than iterative retrieval methods. 3. The controlled head-to-head - where it gets honest Here is where the story gains nuance. A 2025 study from Michigan State and Meta ran RAG against four GraphRAG families under one unified protocol — identical chunking, embeddings, and generation — and found no single winner. The two approaches are complementary: On single-hop, factual lookup (natural questions), plain RAG edged ahead (F1 64.8 vs. 63.0 for the best graph method). On multi-hop reasoning (MultiHop-RAG), graph-guided retrieval pulled in front (70.3 vs. 67.0 overall accuracy). The lesson: A context graph is not a universal upgrade. It is a specialized one that pays off precisely when questions demand reasoning across pieces. 4. When to use graphs: The task-type verdict The most recent benchmark, GraphRAG-Bench (ICLR 2026), set out to answer “In which scenarios do graph structures provide measurable benefits?” Its accuracy-by-task numbers map the boundary cleanly: Simple fact retrieval: Text chunks 60.9 vs. graph 60.1 — effectively a tie. The graph’s structure is overhead the query doesn’t need. Complex reasoning: Graph 53.4 vs. chunks 42.9 — a +10 point graph win. Contextual summarization: Graph 64.4 vs. chunks 51.3 — a +13 point graph win. The scorecard Read top to bottom, the pattern is unmistakable: The graph’s advantage grows with the reasoning depth of the question, while text chunks hold their ground on isolated facts. The catch: Cost and the LLM-judge problem Two caveats keep this from being a slam dunk, and ignoring them is how teams end up disappointed. Building the graph is expensive. Having an LLM extract entities and relationships from an entire corpus isn’t cheap. One analysis put index construction at roughly $48 against GPT-4o for a moderate corpus, far above a vanilla vector index. (Microsoft’s own follow-up, LazyGraphRAG, defers extraction to query time and cuts that to around 0.1% of the cost - a tacit admission that the original budget is impractical for many deployments.) Many of the wins are judged by another LLM — and LLM judges are biased. An independent audit found systematic flaws in this evaluation style: position bias (swapping which answer appears first can swing the win-rate by more than 30 points), length bias , and trial bias (identical comparisons disagree across runs). After correction, one popular method’s reported 66.7% win rate fell to about 39% — below the 50% break-even line. The takeaway is not “the research is wrong.” It is that the large gains — the +20% multi-hop accuracy, the +15-to-30-point recall jumps — are robust, while narrow comprehensiveness margins deserve a skeptical second look with reference-based metrics. So when should you reach for a context graph? Strip away the hype and the decision is refreshingly practical. Use a context graph when: Your questions are multi-hop, global, or sensemaking in nature; you need comprehensive, multi-perspective answers; and your corpus is richly interconnected (research libraries, case files, incident histories, knowledge bases). Stick with text chunks when: Your queries are mostly single-fact lookups; your corpus is small or flat; and indexing cost, latency, and operational simplicity outweigh a marginal quality bump. Best of all, go hybrid: The systematic studies converge on the same recommendation: route each query to the right method, or fuse evidence from both. Combining graph and chunk retrieval consistently beats either one alone. You don’t have to choose a religion; you have to build a router. The bottom line A context graph is not magic, and it is not snake oil. It is a targeted instrument. Hand it a question that requires connecting scattered facts or synthesizing a whole corpus, and it will outperform text chunks decisively. Hand it “what’s the phone number on page 3,” and you’ve paid for indexing you didn’t need. The teams that win with GraphRAG in 2026 won’t be the ones who graph everything. They’ll be the ones who know which questions deserve a graph — and build pipelines smart enough to tell the difference. Dattaraj Rao is an R&D architect at Persistent Systems

articles.title: AMD's upcoming Zen 6 processors could fix microstutters and improve 1% lows in games — Next-gen CPUs tipped to feature per-core optimizations for thermal and power budgets
articles.text:
AMD's upcoming Zen 6 processors could fix microstutters and improve 1% lows in games — Next-gen CPUs tipped to feature per-core optimizations for thermal and power budgets
It's the small things that matter.
AMD is expected to unveil its next-gen Zen 6 platform at CES 2026 with Ryzen 10000 series processors. While we're looking forward to IPC and clock speed improvements, it seems like more subtle, under-the-hood changes could end up upgrading the gaming experience in a big way. According to a tip received by Videocardz, AMD is implementing various per-core optimizations to ensure foreground tasks get priority over background applications. Each new feature is supposed to more smartly manage the power and thermal budgets at the silicon's disposal, so let's go over each of them.
First up, we have CPPC Performance Priority — CPPC stands for Collaborative Processor Performance Control, and it's responsible for communication between the silicon and the OS. It lets the firmware sitting in between decide the performance of each core separately. This feature has actually existed since the Ryzen 3000 series, but it doesn't work perfectly. Zen 6 CPUs are apparently supposed to apply a band-aid fix and improve their effectiveness.
Secondly, we have FloorPerf, which acts as a dynamic, targeted power delivery system. It sets a minimum clock speed for all cores that the silicon can clock down to in case of thermal throttling. For instance, imagine you're running a game in the foreground while Discord and Spotify sit in the background. The temperatures on your Zen 6 CPU rise to the point of throttling, but instead of reducing the speed of all cores, FloorPerf will target the cores running the background tasks first, in order to maintain the performance of your game.
We covered a recent fix like this for the Linux world as well, where a sudden spike in the background can cause the foreground task to choke. Linux has an issue with priority allocation across tasks, so that was a different situation, but similar logic applies here. On a Zen 6 CPU, instead of your game suddenly experiencing microstutters because of aggressive throttling, FloorPerf will try to limit whatever's running in the background first. The aforementioned CPPC Performance Priority should work hand in hand with this feature to maintain clocks on the important cores.
CPPC will get another boost in the form of HighestFreq, which will allow the OS to access more granular chip data to make better core management decisions. As the name suggests, it pertains to maintaining high clock speeds on the cores running a foreground task. The OS will be aware of exactly which core can boost the highest and maintain that speed the longest. This will allow it to assign, for instance, a game's main rendering thread to the fastest cores, while pushing background apps to more power-efficient ones.
In conjunction with this, Zen 6 is also seemingly getting per-core EPP boost. EPP stands for Energy Performance Preference, and it's supposed to fix core parking issues caused by a momentary bottleneck. For example, if the CPU is waiting for the GPU to render the next frame, the clock speeds for the active cores will drop in that moment and struggle to ramp back up in time, forcing all cores to boost when the frame is ready. EPP boost is supposed to identify the active cores and individually keep them in high-performance mode to eliminate any wait times.
Lastly, Zen 6 is reportedly introducing PQOS Global Bandwidth Enforcement and an updated IBS Memory Profiler. Both of these target memory bandwidth with the same goal of maximum stability as everything else discussed so far. The former is responsible for allocating RAM to background tasks, ensuring their usage stays under the limit for foreground priority. The latter will limit L3 cache access to background tasks when it detects that those tasks are slowing down the foreground application, which should help with frametime consistency in games.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
As you can tell, all of these optimizations are supposed to work together and harmonize into a more efficient processor at the end — one that maximizes the silicon's potential as much as possible. Of course, none of this is confirmed and there's a lot that could be gated behind product segmentation. We could see some features only on high-end parts, while some are limited to mobile; there's no telling at the moment, but it's exciting stuff, nonetheless. Seems like a battle for the ages is brewing between Nova Lake and Zen 6 next year.

articles.title: After users 'violate' Google's policies with misinformation, it pulls AI image generation from Google Earth 'while we work on implementing stronger guardrails'
articles.text:
Google pulling Nano Banana from Google Earth after one day shows how bad our AI misinformation problem has got
That didn't last long
We're now well past the point where it's very difficult, and in some cases impossible, to tell AI-generated photos and videos from the real thing. That means it's now important to treat everything you see online from untrusted sources with a big dose of skepticism.
A newly rolled out Google Earth feature has apparently made AI-generated misinformation even more of a problem — and it highlights the scary potential of the technology, as well as the need for stronger guardrails to block the efforts of those who will instantly try and find the most subversive and harmful ways to use a new product.
The feature is AI image generation in Google Earth, powered by the Nano Banana 2 model, and after a wave of inappropriate images were created and posted online, it's now been pulled while Google works on some more robust protections against misinformation.
Google Earth's new feature
It all started with the usual level of hype that Google builds around any new AI feature: the Nano Banana 2 image generation model that has already wowed us in the Gemini app would be available inside Google Earth on the web.
"Generate custom images to help you visualize history, create real estate plans, and more," Google said. "For the first time, you can generate custom images using Google Earth's satellite, aerial, and 3D imagery alongside Nano Banana, which creates concepts grounded in the real world."
Google had examples of how it could be used too: create an infographic about the Statue of Liberty, visualize your dream home by the lake, see what your neighborhood might look like a hundred years from now, or imagine Pompeii just before it got buried by ash and rock from an erupting Mount Vesuvius.
All it took was a text prompt, and Google Earth would combine existing satellite and 3D data to create the AI image you were asking for. While the AI model wasn't new, adding it to the accurate and authentic imagery already in Google Earth was.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
What went wrong
Perhaps we should've seen this coming — and indeed some people did — but combining AI with the 3D data and satellite imagery of Google Earth didn't work out quite as well as Google hoped. The new upgrade was quickly used to create all manner of deceptive images that were then widely shared online.
I'm reluctant to point you to them directly and give these fakes any more attention, but they're not hard to find on social media. Think natural disasters, terrorism attacks, giant sinkholes, alien activity, and refugee populations all in places where they never actually were, thanks to AI.
Some of the images are clearly jokes, but many were produced deliberately to spread misinformation and confusion. That they were based on actual images sourced from Google Earth added extra credibility they wouldn't otherwise have had. And that was enough for Google to remove the feature.
Google says a flood of images "that appear to violate our policies" mean that "we're rolling back this feature in Google Earth while we work on implementing stronger guardrails". The company added:."It's important to note that generated images didn't appear in the main Google Earth experience for others to see and were watermarked as AI generated."
Our AI-filled future
You don't have to look for long online to find rather strong anti-AI sentiment building up among users, especially when it comes to image and video content. The general sentiment on Reddit is that there's "zero use" to a feature like this, and that users are fed up with AI being "shoved down our throats".
There are various obvious lessons to be learned here: firstly not everything needs to have an AI prompt box or an AI element to it, and if some tools are largely AI-free, that's fine. Microsoft recently rolled back some of the AI it added to Notepad — an app where a big part of the appeal is its simplicity — after user complaints.
Secondly, before companies release any new AI features, they need to consider the worst-case scenarios in terms of how they're going to be used. The internet as a collective is going to immediately try and stress test them in the most deceptive and unwholesome ways, and there need to be safety measures put in place around that.
Lastly, it's never been more important to stick to sources of information that you know you can trust: not random social media accounts, but established publications that have policies around AI and its use. That's one effective way you can tell the difference between what's trustworthy and what isn't.

articles.title: DJI Lito 1 (DJI RC-N3) à 320 € au lieu de 379 €
articles.text:
Pour ceux qui veulent s'initier à la prise de vue aérienne sans investir dans un modèle professionnel, le DJI Lito 1 coche déjà beaucoup de cases. Lancé en 2026 comme nouvelle porte d'entrée de la marque, ce drone profite d'une remise sur Amazon : 320 € au lieu de 379 € avec sa radiocommande RC-N3.
Le DJI Lito 1 remplace la gamme Mini d'entrée de gamme de DJI, avec un capteur CMOS de 1/2 pouce capable de capturer des photos en 48 Mpx et des vidéos 4K jusqu'à 100 images par seconde en 10 bits. Pesant moins de 250 g, il entre dans la catégorie C0 en Europe, ce qui lui permet de voler dans de nombreuses zones sans autorisation spécifique. Il embarque un gimbal mécanique 3 axes pour stabiliser les prises de vue ainsi qu'une détection d'obstacles omnidirectionnelle, une fonction rare à ce niveau de prix.
Drône DJI Lito 1 à 320 € au lieu de 379 € sur Amazon
Pourquoi choisir ce drône ultra compacte DJI Lito 1 ?
- Une détection d'obstacles omnidirectionnelle rare sur un drone de ce segment de prix
- Un poids sous les 250 g qui simplifie les démarches réglementaires pour voler en Europe
- Une vidéo 4K jusqu'à 100 i/s, suffisante pour des ralentis fluides sans matériel professionnel
Un drone pensé pour simplifier la prise en main
Les tests s'accordent sur un point : ce modèle vise clairement les débutants, avec des modes de vol intelligents comme ActiveTrack 360°, les QuickShots et les MasterShots qui automatisent la réalisation de séquences complexes. La recharge reste également pensée pour la simplicité, avec un temps de charge direct d'environ 73 minutes par batterie, ou 45 minutes via la station de charge dédiée. Plusieurs testeurs soulignent toutefois que l'autonomie réelle en conditions de vol s'établit plutôt autour de 23 minutes, loin des 36 minutes annoncées en théorique, un écart classique sur ce type de drone mais à garder en tête.
Ce que le capteur 1/2 pouce change par rapport à un modèle plus haut de gamme
Comparé au DJI Lito X1, doté d'un capteur plus grand de 1/1,3 pouce et d'un LiDAR frontal, le Lito 1 fait des concessions logiques sur la qualité d'image en conditions de faible luminosité. Un test allemand souligne d'ailleurs que ce modèle vole de façon stable et longtemps, mais montre ses limites sur la qualité d'image et les accessoires disponibles par rapport à des drones plus onéreux. Pour un usage occasionnel de captation de vacances ou de paysages en plein jour, ces limites restent toutefois peu pénalisantes, la plupart des retours saluant un bon compromis pour découvrir la prise de vue aérienne.
✅ Les points forts
- Détection d'obstacles omnidirectionnelle, rare à ce niveau de prix
- Poids sous les 250 g, simplifiant la réglementation de vol en Europe
- Modes de vol intelligents (ActiveTrack 360°, QuickShots, MasterShots) accessibles aux débutants
❌ Les limites
- Autonomie réelle plus proche de 23 minutes que des 36 minutes annoncées en théorique
- Qualité d'image en faible luminosité en retrait par rapport au DJI Lito X1 ou aux DJI Mini Pro
- Radiocommande RC-N3 fournie nécessite un smartphone pour l'affichage, contrairement à la RC 2 à écran intégré vendue séparément
Drône DJI Lito 1 à 320 € au lieu de 379 € sur Amazon
À 320 €, le DJI Lito 1 avec sa radiocommande RC-N3 reste une porte d'entrée solide dans l'univers du drone DJI, à condition d'accepter les compromis logiques d'un modèle d'entrée de gamme sur l'autonomie réelle et la qualité d'image en basse lumière. Une remise à saisir pour qui veut découvrir la prise de vue aérienne sans investir dans un modèle plus onéreux.
